items.title: Representational Instability in Decoupled Audio Encoders
items.authors: Ehsan Variani(Google Research); Tom Bagby(Google Research); Georg Heigold(Google Research); Ke Wu(Google Research); Cyril Allauzen(Google Research)
items.abstract: Modern audio processing uses neural encoders to generate discrete or continuous representations for downstream models (e.g., LLMs, ASR). While optimized for the Rate-Distortion (RD) trade-off to ensure waveform reconstruction, their stability is often overlooked. We conceptualize the Stability-Rate-Distortion (SRD) trade-off, highlighting representational stability as a third evaluation axis. Optimizing strictly for reconstruction leaves representations vulnerable to acoustic nuisances, creating a Stability Penalty. To evaluate this, we introduce the Continuous Edit Distance (CED) to quantify geometric drift. Analyzing state-of-the-art encoders (EnCodec, SoundStream, Whisper) reveals catastrophic instability. While continuous latents resist minor perturbations, the vector quantization (VQ) bottleneck shatters them into disparate discrete sequences—the Quantization Penalty. Evaluating 26 dialects exposes a cross-lingual "Language Tax," where stability collapses on low-resource dialects due to weak linguistic priors. High waveform fidelity is empirically at odds with representational stability in low-bitrate regimes, highlighting a critical vulnerability in current audio tokens.

items.title: DTM-Codec: Dynamic Token Masking for VFR Speech Coding with Efficient Boundary Selection
items.authors: Hoyeol Sohn(KAIST); Juhan Nam(KAIST)
items.abstract: Variable frame rate (VFR) coding has recently emerged in neural speech codecs, allocating fewer frames to redundant regions and more frames to rapidly changing speech. VFR must transmit side information about retained time steps, but prior gains are either not rigorously addressed or often minor once these overhead bits are included in total bitrate. We present Dynamic Token Masking (DTM)-Codec, a neural speech codec that demonstrates clear gains over fixed-frame-rate baselines under a strict matched-total-bitrate protocol. DTM keeps selected encoder tokens, fills masked positions with a learned <MASK> embedding, and transmits a binary keep-mask for position-aware decoding. We further introduce Path Length Equalization (PLE), a linear-time boundary selector for VFR coding that yields well-spread adaptive segments with negligible overhead. Across operating points, DTM-Codec broadly improves reconstruction quality and intelligibility over fixed-frame-rate baselines.

items.title: HARP: Harmonic-Aware Residual Partitioning for Neural Audio Codecs
items.authors: Qiaoyu Yang(Georgia Institute of Technology); Lixing He(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Tencent Music Entertainment); Binyue Deng(Georgia Institute of Technology); Weifeng Zhao(Tencent Music Entertainment)
items.abstract: Neural audio codecs with residual vector quantization (RVQ) normally treat all frequencies uniformly, so their codebooks become spectrally entangled. Truncating stages then removes an unpredictable mix of frequencies. Parallel band decomposition addresses this by splitting audio into independent bands, but fragments the latent space and loses cross-frequency coherence. We introduce HARP (Harmonic-Aware Residual Partitioning), a training strategy that partitions RVQ stages into frequency-ordered groups where each group refines its target band while the decoder retains access to all lower frequencies. Overtones are reconstructed in the context of their fundamentals, preserving coherence that parallel methods lose. HARP requires no architectural changes; it only modifies the training loss, leaving inference identical to standard RVQ. On speech, music, and general audio, HARP outperforms both standard RVQ and parallel decomposition. MUSHRA listening tests also show perceptual improvements.

items.title: Sleep Sound Event Detection Powered by Learnable Multi-Resolution Adaptive Line Enhancer
items.authors: Chanwoo Park(Korea University); Chanwoo Kim(Korea University)
items.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing, including snoring, hypopnea, and obstructive apnea, is the hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea, whose severity is quantified by the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). As conventional polysomnography is costly and clinically demanding, microphone-only detection has emerged as a noninvasive alternative for screening. We propose ALE-Confidence Fusion Sound Event Detection (ACF-SED), the first framework that directly injects the per-frame confidence map of an Adaptive Line Enhancer (ALE) into Transformer attention biasing and feature modulation, rather than as mere preprocessing. A Multi-Resolution ALE Bank aggregates three parallel NLMS filters at distinct decorrelation delays, while a Confidence-Guided Cross-Path block couples event and noise streams via gated cross-attention. On the Audio-Polygraphy Dataset for Sleep Apnea Analysis, ACF-SED achieves state-of-the-art detection across Event-F1, Segment-F1, and PSDS, enabling end-to-end AHI estimation.

items.title: Similarity as Evidence: An Explainable Siamese Framework for Snore Sound Classification
items.authors: Boyang Meng(Beijing Institute of Technology); Mengkai Sun(Beijing Institute of Technology); Haojie Zhang(Beijing Institute of Technology); Kun Qian(Beijing Institute of Technology); Wei Xue(Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Bin Hu(Beijing Institute of Technology); Björn W. Schuller(TUM University Hospital)
items.abstract: Snore sounds are clinically informative acoustic biomarkers, yet robust and transparent automatic classification remains challenging. We propose an explainable Siamese framework for four-class snore classification that treats similarity as decision evidence. A lightweight convolution module learns ℓ₂-normalised embeddings using joint semi-hard triplet and class-balanced cross-entropy training. Classification is performed via a non-parametric Class Centroid aligned with metric learning. A support-based explanation mechanism relates predictions to reference examples and visually comparable time-frequency activation patterns. On the Munich-Passau Snore Sound Corpus, macro-recall improves from 0.401 (wav2vec2) to 0.638 and remains robust under additive noise. Deletion and perturbation tests validate explanation faithfulness and stability, demonstrating interpretable similarity-based reasoning for clinical sleep assessment.

items.title: Beyond Deep Learning: Speech Segmentation and Phone Classification with Neural Assemblies
items.authors: Trevor Adelson(The University of Melbourne); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Deep learning dominates speech processing but relies on massive datasets, backpropagation, and produces dense representations. Assembly Calculus (AC), which models sparse neuronal assemblies with Hebbian plasticity and winner-take-all competition, offers a biologically grounded alternative. We introduce an AC-based speech processing framework that operates directly on continuous speech by combining three key contributions: (i) neural encoding that converts speech into assembly-compatible spike patterns; (ii) a multi-area architecture organising assemblies across hierarchical timescales and classes; and (iii) cross-area update schemes. Applied to two tasks of boundary detection and segment classification, our framework detects phone (F1=0.69) and word (F1=0.61) boundaries without weight training and achieves 47.5% and 45.1% accuracy on phone and command recognition. These results show that AC-based dynamical systems are a promising alternative to deep learning for speech.

items.title: Positioning Effect of Syllable Shortening on Speech Segmentation: Evidence from Mandarin Listeners
items.authors: Shu-Chen Ou(National Sun Yat-sen University)
items.abstract: This study examines how syllable shortening influences speech segmentation using an artificial language experiment. While listeners use transitional probabilities and salient prosodic cues, reduced prosody such as syllable shortening remains understudied. Native Mandarin listeners (N = 120) learned trisyllabic artificial words under conditions shortening either the initial, middle, or final syllable. Results showed that middle-syllable shortening facilitated segmentation, final-syllable shortening hindered it, and initial shortening had no clear effect. The findings indicate that durational reduction aids segmentation when aligned with predictable word internal structure but disrupts it when applied at word boundaries.

items.title: Perceptual Trade-offs Across Segmental and Suprasegmental Levels: Comparing Ganong Patterns in Mandarin Consonants and Lexical Tones
items.authors: Jiaxin LI(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yi Weng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yicheng Rong(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Gang Peng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: The Ganong effect shows how lexical knowledge biases the perception of ambiguous speech, yet whether this mechanism generalizes across segmental and suprasegmental levels remains unclear. Using a within-subject design (N = 57), we compared acoustic-phonetic processing (identification slopes) and lexical reliance (Ganong effect) for Mandarin tones and consonants. Across levels, neither measure was reliably correlated within individuals, indicating that both capacities are largely level-specific. Yet the underlying weighting mechanism was shared: at both levels, individuals with less precise acoustic-phonetic processing showed a larger Ganong effect. These findings support a reliability-based weighting principle: although the processing resources devoted to specific cues vary across levels, individuals apply a common strategy, weighting lexical knowledge against acoustic-phonetic reliability to resolve ambiguity.

items.title: Rhythmic Patterning in Vietnamese: The Case of Quadrisyllabic Reduplicative Words
items.authors: Phuong Dang(The Ohio State University)
items.abstract: The Vietnamese prosody literature identifies conflicting views on the existence of stress, the pattern of a stress unit, and its prosodic status. This lack of consensus motivated further investigation into rhythmic patterning in Vietnamese. Eight native speakers read a list of eight existing morphosyntactically head-initial and head-final quadrisyllabic reduplicative words, framed in three carrier sentences varying in the number of syllables before and after the target word. An iambic pattern was observed in syllable duration rather than mean rhyme F0 and intensity ratio. The second and fourth syllables were significantly longer than the first and third, respectively. Different carrier sentences did not change the overall rhythmic pattern. These findings support the presence of word-level stress and iambic rhythm, suggesting the possibility of a foot domain in Vietnamese. However, they do not support the role of morphosyntactic headedness in rhythmic patterning of reduplicative words.

items.title: Can Hands Articulate? Kinematic, Acoustic, and Perceptual Analyses of Vowel Production via External Resonators in Kaxi
items.authors: Jinyang Ren(Peking University); Bingliang Zhao(Peking University); Jiangping Kong(Peking University); Xiyu Wu(Peking University)
items.abstract: The source-filter model is foundational in speech science, but the potential for external filters to replace the vocal tract remains underexplored. This research investigates Kaxi, a Chinese folk art in which a reed serves as the source and hand movements act as an external resonator. Kinematic, acoustic, and perceptual analyses of five Kaxi vowels were performed to determine whether hands can articulate intelligible speech. Kinematic tracking reveals that hand postures create a distinct spatial map analogous to tongue-based vowel spaces. Acoustically, Kaxi employs a staircase-like formant tuning strategy to maintain vowel distinctiveness despite high fundamental frequencies. Perceptual evaluations with 24 listeners demonstrate relative robust intelligibility. These results confirm that hands can function effectively as an external speech filter, offering insights into speech plasticity and presenting a potential non-invasive tool for clinical speech rehabilitation.

items.title: Naming Heroes and Villains – The Influence of Phonaesthetics
items.authors: Leonie Schade(Bielefeld University); Daniel Duran(Bielefeld University); Florian Kankowski(Bielefeld University); Joana Cholin(Bielefeld University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University); Christine Mooshammer(Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin)
items.abstract: In constructed languages, creators often represent the personality or character traits of a fictional people linguistically through phonaesthetics, e.g., Tolkien's Orkish, developed to sound harsh and evil, vs. the Elvish languages Sindarin and Quenya, designed to sound elegant and pleasant. The present study investigates whether these design principles are applied to the creation of character names for fictional heroes and villains in German. Participants were asked to invent names for good or evil fictional characters based on two syllable-sized building blocks they selected out of four alternatives. These syllables varied in levels of sonority, nucleus length and CV-complexity. Results show significant differences between the characteristics of syllables selected for naming good and evil characters. GLMERs show significant effects of character (good or evil) on the sonority of syllables selected for naming as well as an influence of the other selected syllable's sonority.

items.title: The Perception of Korean Stop Coda Consonants by Mandarin Speakers in Taiwan: A Comparative Study of Proficiency Levels
items.authors: Shu-Wei Yang(Seoul National University); Jung-yueh Tu(National Chengchi University)
items.abstract: This study investigates the perceptual identification of Korean stop codas (/p, t, k/) by Mandarin speakers in Taiwan, focusing on preceding vowel context and learning experience. Motivated by reports that these learners often produce Korean unreleased codas with audible release, a four-alternative coda identification task was conducted with 30 learners (17 beginners, 13 intermediate learners). Results showed an accuracy hierarchy of /p/ > /t/ > /k/. Vowel context shaped accuracy and confusion patterns: /p/ was best identified after /i/ and /u/, /t/ was best identified after /a/, /t/ was often misperceived as /k/ after non-front vowels (/a, u/), and /k/ showed vowel-dependent confusions. Proficiency group did not significantly affect accuracy, indicating no reliable beginner-intermediate difference in the present sample and task. These findings suggest the need for targeted perceptual training that integrates vowel context and unreleased coda contrasts in Korean teaching.

items.title: Returning the Turn: Do Backchannels Pattern More Like Turn-Holds or Turn-Changes Given Preceding Syntactic Completion and Boundary Tones?
items.authors: Ariëlle Reitsema(Leiden University); Matthijs Westera(Leiden University); Yiya Chen(Leiden University); Johanneke Caspers(Leiden University)
items.abstract: Backchannels are short listener response tokens such as "uh-huh" and "yeah" that signal understanding and encourage the speaker to go on. Several backchannel-inviting cues have been identified in the speech signal directly preceding backchannels, including low and rising final intonation. Since studies on intonation and turn-taking in Dutch have previously treated backchannels as a subclass of turn holds, backchannel-inviting cues in Dutch still lack clarity. The present study re-examines the place of backchannels in the turn-taking system of Dutch based on their cues, asking the question of whether they more closely resemble turn holds or changes in terms of immediately preceding boundary tones and syntactic completion. The results show that backchannels pattern differently from both turn holds and changes, while showing a relatively closer resemblance to the latter category.

items.title: Improving Generalization in Speech Deepfake Detection via Orthogonality-Constrained Common-Specific Feature Decorrelation
items.authors: Donghee Kim(Incheon National University); Wooil Kim(Incheon National University)
items.abstract: Advances in deep learning-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) and Voice Conversion (VC) have enabled highly realistic speech deepfakes, posing serious threats such as fraud and misinformation. Although end-to-end deepfake detection models like RawNet2, RawGAT-ST, and AASIST have been proposed, they often overfit to dataset-specific artifacts under empirical risk minimization. To improve generalization, we propose an orthogonality-based feature decorrelation method for SSL-AASIST, which learns domain-invariant common features that capture consistent authenticity cues and attack-specific specialized features, together with an orthogonality regularization that minimizes their correlation. This encourages the model to rely on consistent authenticity cues rather than domain-dependent shortcuts. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves lower EERs than the baseline across unseen corpora such as 21DF, ASV5, and ITW, confirming improved robustness to unseen domains and spoofing attacks.

items.title: Task-Aware Joint Pruning and Distillation for Efficient Audio Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Miao He(Zhejiang University); Peng Cheng(Zhejiang University; Hangzhou High-Tech Zone (Binjiang) Institute of Blockchain and Data Security); Zhongjie Ba(Zhejiang University; Hangzhou High-Tech Zone (Binjiang) Institute of Blockchain and Data Security); Qing Wen(Zhejiang University); Li Lu(Zhejiang University; Hangzhou High-Tech Zone (Binjiang) Institute of Blockchain and Data Security); Xin Yang(China University of Petroleum (East China)); Kui Ren(Zhejiang University; Hangzhou High-Tech Zone (Binjiang) Institute of Blockchain and Data Security; Shanghai Institute for Advanced Study, Zhejiang University)
items.abstract: Advances in speech synthesis have made deepfake speeches increasingly convincing, posing growing threats to security. While self-supervised learning (SSL) based detectors achieve state-of-the-art performance, their computational demands (typically 300M+ parameters) prevent deployment on resource-constrained devices. Existing compression methods, designed mainly for content-centric tasks, struggle to maintain competitive performance when directly adapted to deepfake detection. We propose a Task-Aware Joint Pruning and Distillation framework that combines cross-domain knowledge distillation with movement-guided structured pruning to transfer forgery-discriminative knowledge and preserve critical structures under aggressive compression. Our framework reduces the model to 31.9M parameters with 6.3x FLOPs reduction, with an average performance drop of only 1.30% across multiple datasets compared to the uncompressed baseline, demonstrating strong potential for on-device deployment.

items.title: ADD-DINO: A Two-Stage Self-Distillation Framework for Audio Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Zhaorui Sun(Xinjiang University; Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd. ); Yihao Chen(University of Science and Technology of China; Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd.); Qiao Chen(University of Science and Technology of China; Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd.); Minqiang Xu(Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd.); Sian Fang(Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd.); Lin Liu(Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd.); Jianbo Zhan(Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd.); Yan Song(University of Science and Technology of China); Guoping Hu(Hefei iFly Digital Technology Co. Ltd.); Lirong Dai(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: This paper proposes ADD-DINO, a two-stage framework aimed at alleviating label scarcity and improving cross-domain generalization in audio deepfake detection. In the first stage, the model is pretrained in a self-supervised manner on 1 million unlabeled audio samples using a non-contrastive teacher-student self-distillation scheme: the teacher branch takes a global long segment, the student branch takes a noise-augmented local short segment, and global-local consistency is learned by aligning their representations. In the second stage, the pretrained teacher backbone is fine-tuned on labeled data for the detection task. Experiments show that on ASVspoof 2019 LA, ADD-DINO achieves performance comparable to a fully supervised baseline using only 20% of the labeled data, and exhibits stronger crossdomain generalization on benchmarks such as In-the-Wild and DFADD. For unseen synthesis methods (e.g., CosyVoice and F5-TTS), ADD-DINO yields a 19.99% relative reduction in EER and a 22.7% improvement in accuracy over the baseline.

items.title: FakeSound2: A Benchmark for Explainable, Traceable, and Generalizable Deepfake Sound Detection
items.authors: Zeyu Xie(Peking University; Tencent AI Lab); Yaoyun Zhang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Xuenan Xu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yongkang Yin(Peking University); Chenxing Li(Tencent AI Lab); Mengyue Wu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yuexian Zou(Peking University)
items.abstract: The growth of audio generation has brought ethical and security concerns over deepfakes, making deepfake detection critical to preventing the malicious misuse of such technologies. Existing methods largely focus on binary classification but fall short in explaining how audio is manipulated, tracing origins, or generalizing to unseen sources, limiting the explainability and reliability of detection. To address these issues, we present FakeSound2, a benchmark designed to advance deepfake sound detection beyond binary accuracy. It evaluates models across three dimensions: localization, traceability, and generalization, covering 6 manipulation types and 12 sources. Experiments reveal that existing models struggle to recognize forgery patterns, provide reliable explanations, and generalize well. FakeSound2 serves as a comprehensive benchmark that highlights key challenges and promotes the development of explainable, traceable, and generalizable methods for trustworthy audio authentication.

items.title: Evidence Subspace Projection: Measuring How Much Evidence Explains Deepfake Detection in Self-Supervised Speech Models
items.authors: Yixuan Xiao(University of Stuttgart); Cheng-Wei Lin(University of Stuttgart); Xin Wang(National Institute of Informatics); Yassine El Kheir(German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)); Arnab Das(German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)); Tim Polzehl(German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)); Sebastian Möller(Technical University of Berlin); Ngoc Thang Vu(University of Stuttgart)
items.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) models are widely used as feature extractors for state-of-the-art audio deepfake detection, but it remains unclear how to directly and quantitatively connect what SSL models capture to detection decisions. To address this gap, we propose Evidence Subspace Projection, a method that represents both evidence factors (e.g., attack category, codec, gender, transmission) and authenticity labels in a shared space constructed from SSL models' neuron activation patterns. By projecting the decision vector onto each evidence subspace, we obtain a scalar ratio that quantifies the explanatory power of each evidence type. We evaluate SSL models in raw, fine-tuned, and post-trained settings on multiple datasets. The results confirm findings from established studies, validating the proposed method, and reveal new insights into model behavior.

items.title: Towards Robust Speech Deepfake Detection via Human-Inspired Reasoning
items.authors: Artem Dvirniak(MIRAI); Evgeny Kushnir(AXXX; HSE; Applied AI Institute); Dmitrii Tarasov(HSE; Applied AI Institute); Artem Iudin(MTUCI); Oleg Kiriukhin(City University of Hong Kong); Mikhail Pautov(AXXX; Trusted AI Research Center); Dmitrii Korzh(AXXX; Applied AI Institute; MTUCI); Oleg Rogov(AXXX; Applied AI Institute; MTUCI)
items.abstract: The modern generative audio models can be used by an adversary in an unlawful manner, specifically, to impersonate other people to gain access to private information. To mitigate this issue, speech deepfake detection (SDD) methods started to evolve. Unfortunately, current SDD methods generally suffer from the lack of generalization to new audio domains and generators. More than that, they lack interpretability, especially human-like reasoning that would naturally explain the attribution of a given audio to the bona fide or spoof class and provide human-perceptible cues. In this paper, we propose HIR-SDD, a novel SDD framework that combines the strengths of Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) with the chain-of-thought reasoning derived from the novel proposed human-annotated dataset. Experimental evaluation demonstrates both the effectiveness of the proposed method and its ability to provide reasonable justifications for predictions.

items.title: Physics-Aware Deepfake Detection via Distance–Speech Consistency
items.authors: Kyeongrae Kim(KAIST); Kim Sung-Bin(POSTECH); Oh Hyun-Bin(POSTECH); Tae-Hyun Oh(KAIST)
items.abstract: Recent progress in generative models has made talking-head deepfakes highly realistic and easy to create, jeopardizing public trust. However, most audio-visual deepfake detectors rely on lip-speech synchronization and are designed for static, frontal videos, limiting their reliability in dynamic, in-the-wild recordings where the speaker moves and lip cues are degraded or missing. As an alternative, we propose a physics-aware detector for dynamic speaking videos that leverages an acoustic constraint: in real recordings, speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance, whereas deepfake generation can break this coupling. Our method combines distance estimates from video with distance-dependent acoustic measures from speech to detect deepfakes. Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show that the proposed physical cue is effective in dynamic scenarios, and that it complements lip-sync-based detectors, with a simple ensemble achieving consistent gains across datasets. Codes are available at https://byulharang.github.io/PADD/.

items.title: MS-GNN: Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network for Detecting Local Audio-Visual Forgery Traces
items.authors: Jianrong Wang(Tianjin University; Tianjin Renai College); Hengyang Guo(Tianjin University); Jie Liu(Tianjin Electronic Information College); Ju Zhang(Tianjin University of Technology); Qi Li(Tianjin University); Ying Guo(Tianjin University); Jing Zhao(Tianjin Beiyang Rongke Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: The proliferation of audio-visual deepfake technology poses a threat to social trust. Approaches relying on globally pooled multimodal features can dilute transient forgery traces (e.g., lip-sync misalignments). We propose MS-GNN, a multi-scale graph neural network for audio-visual deepfake detection. MS-GNN partitions the audio-visual stream into windows to capture local traces. We use a multi-scale graph: a bottom-up pathway aggregates window features into segment-level semantics, while a top-down pathway propagates global context to refine local evidence. We obtain a global video representation by aggregating window features, and train with window-level (auxiliary) and video-level (main) supervision. Experiments on LAV-DF and FakeAVCeleb show that MS-GNN improves deepfake detection, particularly for videos with localized forgery traces. The source code will be available here.

items.title: Referee: Reference-aware Audiovisual Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Hyemin Boo(Ewha Womans University); Eunsang Lee(Ewha Womans University); Jiyoung Lee(Ewha Womans University)
items.abstract: Deepfakes have rapidly posed serious threats from advanced generative models, yet audiovisual deepfake detection approaches still struggle to generalize to unseen manipulation methods. We propose a novel reference-aware audiovisual deepfake detection method, called Referee, to capture fine-grained identity discrepancies. Referee employs identity bottleneck and matching modules to model the relational consistency of speaker-specific cues captured by a single one-shot example as a biometric anchor. Extensive experiments on FakeAVCeleb, FaceForensics++, and KoDF demonstrate that Referee achieves state-of-the-art results on cross-dataset and cross-language evaluation protocols. These results highlight that explicitly correlating reference-based biometric priors is a key frontier for achieving reliable audiovisual forensics. The code is available at https://github.com/ewha-mmai/referee.

items.title: OPERA-Net: Octave-aware Phase-sensitive Enhanced Recognition Architecture for Singing Voice Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Fengwei Ye(Sun Yat-sen University); Kun Zeng(Sun Yat-sen University)
items.abstract: The proliferation of high-fidelity singing voice synthesis requires robust Singing Voice Deepfake Detection (SVDD) countermeasures. However, state-of-the-art speech spoofing detectors degrade significantly when applied to singing. This vulnerability arises from dense background music (BGM) interference and reliance on magnitude spectra, which discard critical phase discontinuities. To address these, we propose OPERA-Net, a novel dual-stream architecture for SVDD. We introduce a Phase-Consistent CQT (PC-CQT) representation that models instantaneous frequency derivatives to capture phase anomalies. A Semantic-Guided Gating mechanism leverages pre-trained WavLM semantic priors to filter the PC-CQT stream, isolating vocal forgery traces from BGM. Cross-corpus evaluations on the CtrSVDD and SingFake datasets show OPERA-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance, with superior generalization over existing baselines.

items.title: A Training-Free Proactive Defense Against Partial Speech Manipulation via Self-Embedding Steganography
items.authors: Yigitcan Özer(National Institute of Informatics); Zhe Zhang(National Institute of Informatics); Wanying Ge(National Institute of Informatics); Xin Wang(National Institute of Informatics); Junichi Yamagishi(National Institute of Informatics)
items.abstract: Partial deepfake speech, where only limited segments of an utterance are synthesized or manipulated, poses a significant challenge to existing deepfake detection systems. As the proportion of spoofed regions decreases, passive detectors become increasingly unreliable, and accurate detection and restoration remain challenging. In this paper, we revisit audio steganography from a new perspective and propose its use as a proactive defense against partially deepfaked audio. In particular, we consider a self-embedding strategy in which a clean speech signal embeds a compressed representation of itself, enabling post-hoc extraction of reference content. We demonstrate how existing audio steganography methods can be repurposed to support detection of partial deepfakes through codec-based restoration. Experiments on a benchmark dataset show that the proposed approach complements passive defenses. Remarkably, the proposed method operates without any training, providing a robust and data-efficient alternative for partial deepfake detection.

items.title: Consistency-Regularized Dual-Branch Network with Performance-Aware Mean Teacher for Sound Event Detection
items.authors: Lipeng Dai(University of Science and Technology of China); Qing Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Wu Guo(University of Science and Technology of China); Peng Gao(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhijun Zhang(University of Science and Technology of China); Kuiliang Li(University of Science and Technology of China); Jinjie Fu(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a method to enhance pre-trained model-based sound event detection. The model architecture consists of a pre-trained Audio Teacher Student Transformer (ATST) front-end and a cascaded dual-branch back-end that models shallow and deep features of ATST, respectively. To capture more discriminative cues, we propose a temporal topological consistency loss to align the temporal structural similarities of the dual-branch features. For model training, we propose a performance-aware mean teacher framework, which features an adaptive exponential moving average strategy to adjust the teacher model's update magnitude based on the student model's performance, thereby ensuring the stability of model updates. Furthermore, we employ a cross-stage fusion strategy to combine the strengths of different training stages. Experimental results on the DCASE 2024 Challenge Task 4 dataset demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

items.title: MixProLAP: Mixture-Induced Uncertainty Modeling for Probabilistic Language-Audio Pretraining
items.authors: Yu Nakagome(LINE WORKS Corporation); Jaesong Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Soo-Whan Chung(NAVER Cloud Corporation)
items.abstract: Acoustic environments often contain multiple overlapping sound events, and the same acoustic scene can be described using diverse textual expressions, making audio-text alignment inherently ambiguous. This paper proposes a probabilistic audio-language pretraining framework to model many-to-many correspondence ambiguity in audio-text alignment. Unlike conventional contrastive methods that learn deterministic point embeddings, our approach represents each modality as a distribution and learns uncertainty-aware cross-modal alignment. Rather than relying on masking-based uncertainty simulation, we mix audio-text pairs to create overlapping sounds that better reflect real acoustic mixtures and capture semantic inclusion relations among sound events. We further introduce a multi-level inclusion loss to enforce representations consistent with these relations. Experiments on audio-text retrieval benchmarks show that the proposed method outperforms deterministic baselines.

items.title: UD-ASD: A Unified Diffusion Model for Anomalous Sound Detection
items.authors: Pengxiang Gao(University of Science and Technology of China); Yu Qiu(University of Science and Technology of China); Yanzhi Song(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: Anomalous Sound Detection (ASD) aims to determine whether faults have occurred by monitoring sounds. Existing methods detect a limited range of anomalies, exhibit poor generalization, or train a separate model for each machine. Diffusion models possess strong generalization and can generate specific data with condition guidance. We propose a unified diffusion model only with a small module. The audio is first transformed into log-Mel spectrograms. The lightweight module embeds machine IDs into condition embeddings, guiding the model to reconstruct data for specific machines. Then diffusion model reconstructs data with condition, using Gaussian Mixture Models to fit the distributions of reconstruction errors. Our unified model could monitor multiple machine types and learn more fundamental feature spaces with cross-domain learning. Experiments on DCASE2022 Challenge Task 2 show that our model achieves 3.44% AUC and 2.52% pAUC improvements over baseline, validating its effectiveness.

items.title: A Semantic-Anchor-based Method for Open-Vocabulary Sound Event Detection
items.authors: Jun Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Pengfei Cai(University of Science and Technology of China); Yanfeng Shi(University of Science and Technology of China); Qing Gu(University of Science and Technology of China); Nan Jiang(University of Science and Technology of China); Lirong Dai(University of Science and Technology of China); Yan Song(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: Recent query-based open-vocabulary sound event detection (SED) is promising beyond closed-set models. Yet most methods only use query vectors for retrieval without semantic understanding of events, thus limiting recognition of novel classes. To tackle this, we propose a semantic-anchor-based method. Specifically, we learn a set of semantic anchor vectors to serve as semantic-level reference tokens, so arbitrary events can be better understood by attending to the anchors. We also introduce bidirectional-attention to enhance query-feature interaction for more effective retrieval, and design tailored query augmentation to improve robustness. Experiments on AudioSet-Strong show superior accuracy in recognizing novel classes, achieving 34.9 PSDS under the open-vocabulary setting and surpassing prior open-vocabulary SED models. Moreover, cross-dataset evaluation on DESED validates our method's strong generalization, and notably in zero-shot, we achieve 44.1 PSDS1, even surpassing DESED-supervised baseline.

items.title: Cross Domain Few-Shot Class-Incremental Audio Classification Via Adversarial Contrastive Learning
items.authors: Yongjie Si(South China University of Technology); Yanxiong Li(South China University of Technology); Sen Huang(South China University of Technology); Beibei Liu(South China University of Technology)
items.abstract: Current Few-shot Class-incremental Audio Classification (FCAC) methods assume that samples of base and incremental classes are in the same domain (following the same distribution). However, there is generally a domain shift between the above two types of samples. In this paper, we explore the problem of Cross Domain FCAC where samples of base and incremental classes have domain shift. We propose a strategy of adversarial contrastive training which enables the model to effectively classify samples of different classes from unseen domains. The model consists of an encoder and a classifier. The encoder is trained in base session but frozen in incremental sessions, whereas the classifier is trained in all sessions. Experiments are done on six pairs of cross-domain datasets. Results show that our method exceeds state-of-the-art methods in average accuracy. The code is at https://github.com/YongjieSi/ACL.

items.title: USV-DETR: High-Resolution and Densely Supervised Detection of Ultrasonic Vocalizations
items.authors: Yilan Wei(Northwestern University); Kumiko Long(Northwestern University); Arielle Granston(Northwestern University); Adrian Rodriguez-Contreras(Northwestern University)
items.abstract: Ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) are important behavioral indicators in rodent neuroscience research, yet automated detection remains challenging due to their small scale, narrow bandwidth, and sparse distribution in spectrograms. Existing methods mostly rely on rule-based tools or traditional convolutional networks, which struggle to preserve critical acoustic details and lack effective mechanisms for modeling fine-grained and sparse acoustic patterns. We propose USV-DETR, an end-to-end model optimized for USV detection. Built on RT-DETR, it introduces a high-resolution P2 feature layer to better represent narrowband, short-duration signals and adopts the DEIM training framework to provide dense and stable supervision for sparse small targets. Experiments across different datasets show that USV-DETR consistently achieves the best detection performance, enabling more precise time-frequency localization of USVs and providing a useful tool for acoustic feature analysis.

items.title: Enhancing Temporal Prediction Consistency for Short-Duration Acoustic Scene Classification via Semantic Adversarial Training
items.authors: Yiqiang Cai(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yizhou Tan(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Peihong Zhang(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yuxuan Liu(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Shengchen Li(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Xi Shao(Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
items.abstract: Short-duration Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) is essential for building responsive environmental sensing systems. However, standard ASC models show severe performance collapse when restricting to short observation windows. Our study reveals that the degradation stems from temporal prediction inconsistency--a misalignment between the long-term scene context and the model's predictions among short observation windows. To address this, we propose the Semantic Adversarial Training (SAT) framework. SAT introduces an auxiliary adversarial objective that competes with the standard scene classification task, forcing the feature extractor to discard duration-dependent semantic variances while learning scene-discriminative features. Experimental results demonstrate a direct correlation between temporal prediction consistency and model accuracy. Crucially, SAT significantly mitigates the performance drop on high-discrepancy samples, yielding a more robust and temporally consistent ASC system.

items.title: BG-CRNN: Boundary-Guided Dynamic Attention for Sound Event Detection in Complex Scenarios
items.authors: Zongmu Lin(Wuhan University); Zhongxin Bai(Harbin Engineering University); Jisheng Bai(Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications); Zhenru Li(Wuhan University); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Jingdong Chen(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jacob Benesty(University of Quebec)
items.abstract: Existing sound event detection (SED) systems often suffer severe performance degradation in complex noisy environments. To address this, we propose a noise-robust Boundary-Guided Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (BG-CRNN). We introduce a dynamic boundary attention module that constructs masks by predicting event boundaries. This restricts self-attention strictly within individual event segments, preventing target sound features from being contaminated by adjacent background noise. Furthermore, a Boundary-Guided Attention (BGA) module utilizes these boundary features to generate gating weights, adaptively enhancing active event regions. Experiments on the WildDESED dataset demonstrate that BG-CRNN consistently outperforms baselines across signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from 10 dB to -5 dB. Notably, it achieves a PSDS1 of 0.191 even under the extreme -5 dB condition, confirming its strong noise robustness.

items.title: Towards Event-Robust Acoustic Scene Classification
items.authors: Yiqiang Cai(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Bohan Hu(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yu Yang(Zhongdian Zhiheng Information Technology Service Co., Ltd); Pengwei Lu(China Telecom Jiangsu Branch); Shengchen Li(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Xi Shao(Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Event-Shifted Acoustic Scene (ESAS) dataset, a novel benchmark for evaluating the robustness of Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) systems against unknown sound events. Existing ASC datasets typically contain recordings of clean and consistent audio, while real-world environments often include diverse and unexpected sound events. To bridge this gap, ESAS simulates real-world acoustic variability by injecting foreground sound events into background scenes with the assistance of large language models. In this work, we present the construction methodology, dataset statistics, and evaluation protocols. Furthermore, a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art ASC systems is conducted using the ESAS benchmark. Experimental results reveal that existing ASC models suffer significant performance degradation when facing the event-shift challenge. The introduction of the ESAS dataset aims to drive future research toward event-robust ASC.

items.title: From Masking to Merging: Rethinking SpecAugment for Efficient Audio Spectrogram Transformer
items.authors: Minhee Park(Korea University); Hyowon Ahn(Korea University); Chanwoo Kim(Korea University)
items.abstract: This paper proposes SpecAugment-Patch Merging, a simple yet effective method to accelerate Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) training. We first apply SpecAugment to mask input spectrograms at the patch level, and after positional embeddings are added, the method selects r pairs of masked patches and merges them, reducing the number of tokens processed by the Transformer. Increasing the number of merged pairs r from 0 to 100 keeps mAP on AudioSet nearly unchanged (34.07 to 34.08) while throughput increases from 43.3 to 49.3 samples/sec, which is a relatively 13.9% improvement. Similar patterns appear on ESC-50 and Speech Commands V2, where throughput steadily improves with only minor accuracy changes, demonstrating that this merging approach provides faster training with minimal performance loss.

items.title: Progressive Learnable Counterfactual Attention for Music Classification
items.authors: Yi-Xing Lin(Academia Sinica); Wen-Li Wei(Academia Sinica); Jia-Ching Wang(National Central University); Jen-Chun Lin(Academia Sinica)
items.abstract: Counterfactual attention learning mitigates biased attention by disentangling task-relevant cues from spurious regions. Learnable Counterfactual Attention (LCA) introduces a learnable counterfactual branch to expose misleading yet discriminative biases during training. However, learning in a single representation space often leaves residual biases entangled with the main attention. We propose Progressive Learnable Counterfactual Attention (P-LCA), a multi-stage framework that refines attention via stage-wise representation projection. After each counterfactual training stage, main-branch attention features are projected into a new latent space, allowing subsequent stages to examine biases from different perspectives and reveal hidden patterns. This design enables thorough and stable debiasing. Experiments on Artist20, GTZAN, and EMOPIA datasets show consistent improvements across music classification tasks, while attention visualizations indicate focused, stable attention patterns.

items.title: Energy Redistribution in the Spectro-Temporal Modulation Domain for Near-End Listening Enhancement
items.authors: Amin Edraki(Huawei CBG); Amirhossein Hajavi(Huawei CBG); Irina Kezele(Huawei CBG); Yuanhao Yu(Huawei CBG)
items.abstract: Near-end listening enhancement (NELE) improves speech intelligibility by modifying speech prior to playback in noisy environments. We propose a NELE algorithm that redisributes speech energy in the spectro-temporal modulation domain rather than the conventional time-frequency domain. A global modulation mask is optimized using an objective measure of speech intelligibility and applied under an energy constraint. An ablation study shows that jointly modifying spectral and temporal modulations results in more consistent gains than single-dimension masking. Evaluation on several noise types demonstrates consistent improvements over established NELE baselines across multiple objective and subjective measures of speech intelligibility.

items.title: End-to-End Model Compression for Personalized Neural Speech Codecs
items.authors: Inseon Jang(ETRI); Minje Kim(UIUC); Wootaek Lim(ETRI); Seungkwon Beack(ETRI)
items.abstract: Neural speech coding (NSC) leverages deep learning to achieve high-quality speech compression, surpassing conventional methods. However, recent NSC models have grown substantially in size and complexity, limiting their feasibility for real-time processing on resource-constrained devices. To address this issue, we propose a speaker-aware model compression framework for end-to-end NSC. In this approach, speakers are clustered by perceptual similarity, and both encoder and decoder are trained with group-specific data, reducing computation while preserving perceptual quality. Subjective listening tests show that the proposed method reduces the model size by 96% and the bitrate by 50% (from 2 kbps to 1 kbps), while maintaining the perceptual quality of the state-of-the-art Descript audio codec (DAC). Moreover, the personalized models remain robust under noisy conditions, consistently outperforming baselines under acoustic distortions. These results highlight the feasibility of deploying NSC on low-power devices in both clean and noisy environments.

items.title: Acoustic and Semantic Feature Fusion Mapping for Lyric Intelligibility Prediction
items.authors: Yuxiang Fu(Tsinghua University); Guodong Lin(Tsinghua University); Da Shen(Tsinghua University); Wenlin Huang(Ministry of Public Security); Weili Jiang(Ministry of Public Security); Kai Gao(Ministry of Public Security); Boyu Zhao(Ministry of Public Security); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Lyric intelligibility, the ease with which listeners understand song lyrics, affects listening experience, memorability, and language learning. We propose a data-driven system extracting acoustic features, and Whisper encoder representations. Feature engineering, including temporal statistics and interactions among correlated features, enhances prediction. A regression module maps features to intelligibility scores using neural models (FCNs, MOE, CNN+GRU, Transformers) and gradient-boosted trees (CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost). Experiments on a manually annotated dataset show gradient-boosted trees outperform neural networks, with CatBoost achieving Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) 27.367 and correlation (Corr) 0.654. Results highlight the effectiveness of structured feature modeling and Whisper-derived representations.

items.title: Screening Matters: A Comparative Study of Conventional and Crowdsourced Listening Tests
items.authors: Anika Treffehn(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS); Andrea Eichenseer(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS); Emily Kratsch(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS); Nicola Pia(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS)
items.abstract: Subjective evaluation remains the most reliable way of testing speech and audio coding techniques. Crowdsourcing the listening task is a cost-efficient and fast way of conducting this evaluation, but the quality of the results tends to be inferior to that of conventional listening tests done in the controlled environment of a laboratory. In this paper, classical and neural speech codecs are evaluated to compare P.808 against P.800 DCR tests. A statistical analysis is conducted to investigate the effectiveness of selected screening methods. The analysis shows that the crowdsourced evaluation can be improved by employing post-screening methods based on anchor ordering and rating span, and continuous screening methods like traps and gold standard questions, thus giving more value to the ratings obtained for the codecs under test. Based on these outcomes, a set of suitable screenings is proposed, for cost-effective, simplified, and bias-free enhancement of listening results.

items.title: Assessing the Impact of Noise and Speech Enhancement on the Intelligibility of Speech Codecs
items.authors: Lyonel Behringer(IIS); Anna Leschanowsky(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS)); Anjana Rajasekhar(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS)); Emily Kratsch(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS)); Guillaume Fuchs(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS))
items.abstract: Preserving speech intelligibility is a minimum requirement for speech codecs in communication. Recently, very low-bitrate neural codecs have gained interest for replacing classical codecs, reinforcing the need to evaluate whether intelligibility is preserved in realistic scenarios. In this paper, we evaluate the intelligibility and listening effort of classical and neural speech codecs in clean and noisy conditions. Further, we assess the impact of speech enhancement (SE) before coding, simulating a possible audio processing pipeline. The results show that classical codecs are more noise robust than neural codecs. Further, SE can lead to significant intelligibility and listening effort improvements for codecs otherwise negatively affected by noise. Listening effort reveals nuanced differences when intelligibility is saturated. Lastly, objective intelligibility based on automatic speech recognition is highly correlated with subjective intelligibility scores averaged per condition.

items.title: Improving Cross-Dataset Speech Intelligibility Prediction for Hearing-Impaired Listeners with Few-Shot Adaptation
items.authors: Guojian Lin(Southern Univ. of Sci. and Tech.); Xuefei Wang(Southern Univ. of Sci. and Tech.); Ryandhimas E. Zezario(Academia Sinica); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Fei Chen(Southern Univ. of Sci. and Tech.)
items.abstract: Speech intelligibility prediction models suffer substantial performance degradation when generalized to unseen datasets. In real-world scenarios, subjective listening evaluations are costly and limited, resulting in scarce labeled data for cross-dataset adaptation, which further challenges the development of accurate and generalizable evaluation models. To address this issue, we propose CFA-SIPNet, a speech intelligibility prediction network for hearing-impaired (HI) listeners based on cross-domain few-shot adaptation with adapter modules and contrastive learning. Experimental results show that CFA-SIPNet achieves a relative RMSE reduction of 8.5% and a relative PCC improvement of 4.2% over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) model in cross-dataset prediction. With less than 20% of target-domain samples, CFA-SIPNet outperforms models trained on the full in-domain target dataset. These results validate the effectiveness of CFA-SIPNet in enhancing cross-dataset generalization.

items.title: Beyond Cross-Reconstruction: Probing-Based Disentanglement Evaluation for Acoustic Teleportation Codecs
items.authors: Philipp Grundhuber(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits); Emanuël A. P. Habets(International Audio Laboratories Erlangen)
items.abstract: Some neural audio codecs disentangle speech into latent subspaces encoding content, speaker identity, and acoustics, enabling acoustic teleportation and voice conversion. Existing evaluations rely on cross-reconstruction quality, which cannot reliably detect leakage across partitions. We extend a probing-based framework to assess disentanglement by regressing room-acoustic parameters (reverberation time, clarity, and direct-to-reverberant ratio) and classifying speaker identity, using the gap between intended and unintended partitions as the disentanglement measure. Applied to an acoustic teleportation codec, we find speaker identity is largely confined to its partition, while acoustics leak into the speech embeddings due to the training objective. Acoustic embeddings blindly estimate room parameters within 0.02 s of supervised baselines, indicating physically meaningful structure emerges without explicit supervision.

items.title: Too Good to Be True: A Study on Modern Automatic Speech Recognition Systems for the Evaluation of Speech Enhancement
items.authors: Danilo Oliveira(University of Hamburg); Tal Peer(University of Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(University of Hamburg)
items.abstract: Speech enhancement (SE) systems are typically evaluated using a variety of instrumental metrics. The use of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to evaluate SE performance is common in literature, usually in terms of word error rate (WER). However, WER scores depend heavily on the choice of ASR system and text normalization pipeline. In this paper, we investigate how modern ASR models correlate with human recognition of enhanced speech. A listening experiment reveals that modern ASR models with large-scale noisy training and embedded language models correlate more with human WER than simpler ones, with a transducer model providing the most reliable transcriptions. Nevertheless, we also show that these models' robustness to noise and use of context can be uninformative to an acoustics-focused evaluation of enhancement performance.

items.title: Probing Low Frame Rate Degradation in Neural Audio Codecs
items.authors: Alex Gichamba(Carnegie Mellon University Africa); Moise Busogi(Carnegie Mellon University Africa)
items.abstract: Low frame rates in neural audio codecs are attractive for autoregressive speech synthesis, where the generation cost scales linearly with the sequence length. Recent work has demonstrated that codecs can operate at 12.5 Hz and below, but the mechanisms underlying low frame rate degradation remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these mechanisms through a controlled frame rate ablation. We reproduce a quality cliff at 6.25 Hz reported in previous works and evaluate candidate explanations: phonemic collisions and codebook saturation, neither of which shows evidence of a fundamental barrier. The cliff is instead caused by suboptimal training configuration: fixed clip duration during training yields too few tokens at low frame rates, starving the decoder of inter-token context. Once corrected, WER degrades smoothly with phonemic load down to 3.1 Hz and 1.6 Hz, suggesting the inference-time efficiency gains of low frame rate codecs are more accessible than previously assumed.

items.title: Deterministic Prompting for Speaker-Stable Low-Resource Greek TTS
items.authors: Georgios Syllas(Athena R.C.); Efthymios Georgiou(University of Bern); Kosmas Kritsis(Athena R.C.); Alexandros Potamianos(National Technical University of Athens)
items.abstract: Modern TTS systems approach human quality for high-resource languages but degrade when clean speech data is scarce. Modern Greek exemplifies this, lacking the curated corpora behind state-of-the-art synthesis. We propose a data curation recipe that transforms audiobook recordings into TTS-ready data via WhisperX alignment and filtering. Then we fine-tune Parler-TTS (880M), a prompt-based multilingual model whose pretraining encodes phonetic priors transferable to Greek. During development, we find that LLM-generated style prompts introduce speaker drift at inference. Replacing them with deterministic prompts resolves this, and a speaker-specific LoRA stage trained on 3.5 h of single-speaker data anchors identity while updating ~5% of parameters. Our system achieves WER 10.7% (2.9 above the ASR floor), MOS-I 4.00 (vs. 4.36 human speech), and near-human speaker consistency (MOS-C 4.24 vs. 4.30), showing that robust single-speaker Greek TTS is achievable with limited curated data.

items.title: DiaMoE-TTS: A Unified IPA-Based Dialect TTS Framework with Parameter-Efficient Adaptation and Reward-Driven Optimization
items.authors: Ziqi Chen(Tsinghua University); Gongyu Chen(Giant Network); Yihua Wang(Giant Network); Zihao Chen(Giant Network); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Dialect speech embodies rich cultural and linguistic diversity, yet building a unified text-to-speech (TTS) system for dialects remains challenging due to scarce data, inconsistent phonetic representations, and dialect interference in joint modeling. We explore a unified dialect TTS pipeline based on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture. A unified International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) front-end is adopted to reduce pronunciation ambiguity across dialects. Built upon the F5-TTS framework, we introduce a dialect-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) text encoder to mitigate style averaging in multidialect training. For low-resource dialect expansion, we employ parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to enable adaptation with only a few hours of speech data. We further investigate incorporating high-quality dialect data into the unified model. Experiments show that GRPO-based reinforcement learning reduces the word error rate (WER) for both the target dialect and several related dialects.

items.title: SALT: Selective Allophone-Level Tokenization for Korean Text-to-Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Kwangsung Kim(CBS; Sogang University); Cellik Adams(Sogang University); EunKyoung Jo(Global Korean Studies, Sogang University)
items.abstract: Recent Korean TTS studies often use direct grapheme input due to the phonetic transparency of the Korean alphabet, Hangul. However, Korean orthography is also morphophonemic, and grapheme sequences do not always correspond to the actual pronunciation. Since the mapping between graphemes, phonemes, and allophones is almost deterministic in the Standard Korean Pronunciation, we propose Selective Allophone-Level Tokenization (SALT), which incorporates a selected set of allophonic phenomena into the input rather than relying on implicit learning by the TTS model. In experiments fine-tuning a pre-trained model, SALT-N, which improves token distributional balance, outperformed baselines. In a 12.75-hour dataset, SALT-N obtained a CER of 3.30% and achieved the highest NMOS, whereas grapheme input resulted in a CER of 4.74%. In an extremely low-resource 1-hour setting, SALT-N was the only method to achieve a CER below 10% (8.19%), whereas all baseline models suffered from severe degradation.

items.title: G2PO: A Lightweight Lexicon-enhanced Framework for Open-Vocabulary Mandarin Polyphone Disambiguation
items.authors: Feifan Chen(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Chunhui Lu(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Rui Zhou(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Liming Song(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Hongjun Kil(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics); YoonChoon Hwang(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics); Junkwang Oh(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics)
items.abstract: Polyphone disambiguation is a crucial component for Chinese Text-to-Speech systems. While recent arts achieve high accuracy using large pre-trained models like BERT, their massive parameter sizes hinder on-device deployment. Furthermore, these closed-set classifiers fail to predict pronunciations unseen during training. To address this, we propose g2pO, a lightweight open-vocabulary framework. It adopts a tiny BERT encoder and fuses external dictionary knowledge into hidden states via a lexicon adapter. Instead of using heavy pre-trained word embeddings to encode dictionary information, our method dynamically constructs word representations from hidden states via mix-pooling. These designs minimize the parameter size and enable generalization to unseen pronunciations. Experiments show with only 3.99M parameters (27x smaller than BERT-based methods), g2pO outperforms previous methods, achieving 99.15% accuracy on the CPP dataset and 70.79% zero-shot accuracy on unseen pronunciations.

items.title: UR-BERT: Scaling Text Encoders for Massively Multilingual TTS Through Universal Romanization and Speech Token Prediction
items.authors: Sangmin Lee(Yonsei University); Eek Gyun Ahn(Yonsei University); Woongjib Choi(Yonsei University); Hong-Goo Kang(Yonsei University)
items.abstract: We propose UR-BERT, a Romanized transcription-based text-to-speech (TTS) encoder for massively multilingual TTS systems. Conventional grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P)-based approaches are limited to around 100 languages due to the availability of reliable G2P resources. In contrast, UR-BERT scales to 495 languages by unifying diverse writing systems into a shared Romanization representation. To further enhance phonetic fidelity and text-speech alignment, we introduce a speech token prediction objective during training, which encourages the encoder to learn speech-aware phonetic representations in a data-efficient manner. Experiments show that TTS systems built on UR-BERT consistently outperform recent text encoder baselines across a wide range of languages and resource conditions, and demonstrate strong generalization to unseen languages.

items.title: Listenability of Synthetic Speech: On the Effect of Linguistic Registers in Text-to-Speech Input
items.authors: Maja Jønck Hjuler(Queensland University of Technology; Université Grenoble Alpes); Tuyet Katie Nhi Tran(Queensland University of Technology); Laurianne Sitbon(Queensland University of Technology)
items.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), LLM-generated text is increasingly being used as input for speech synthesis, yet little is known about its listenability compared to other linguistic registers. This paper presents a preliminary study of listenability across conversational, formal written, simplified written, and LLM-generated registers in terms of listener effort and comprehension during synthesized delivery. An experiment with 47 participants measured subjective mental effort, cognitive load, and cued recall in a within-subjects design. Register characteristics were examined through readability metrics and Biber's Multi-Dimensional Analysis. Our findings indicate higher listenability for synthesized speech from written sources compared to radio transcripts, demonstrating the intricacies of language and register. Furthermore, LLM-generated text was as listenable as Wikipedia-sourced text, supporting its suitability in synthetic speech applications.

items.title: Uncovering the Impact of G2P Precision on Korean TTS: A Large-Scale Statistical Validation via a Novel Morphological Engine
items.authors: Heejo You(Hyundai Motor Group); Sungwoo Moon(Hyundai Motor Group)
items.abstract: Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) conversion is vital for TTS, yet the widely used Korean g2pk library suffers from high latency and inaccurate phonological modeling at word boundaries. Such inaccuracies act as "label noise", degrading TTS performance and training efficiency. To resolve this, we propose a novel rule-based G2P engine featuring an object-oriented data structure with syllable-morpheme connectivity and a recursive re-evaluation mechanism for sequential phonological rules. Rigorous benchmarking shows that the proposed engine significantly outperforms g2pk in both speed (3.14ms vs. 14.98ms, p < 0.001) and accuracy (85.7% vs. 27.2%). Furthermore, large-scale statistical validation via 96 VITS models (32 per condition) demonstrates that our engine achieves statistically significant improvements in intelligibility. The results confirm that our approach enhances not only the final audio quality but also the overall training efficiency of TTS models by providing consistent phonetic representations.

items.title: Phonikud: Overcoming Phonetic Underspecification for Hebrew Text-To-Speech
items.authors: Yakov Kolani(Independent Researcher); Maxim Melichov(Reichman University); Cobi Calev(Cisco Systems); Morris Alper(Tel Aviv University.; CMU)
items.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) for Modern Hebrew is challenged by the language's orthographic complexity, with existing solutions ignoring underspecified phonetic features such as stress. We present a framework for more phonetically accurate Hebrew TTS with four contributions: (1) Phonikud, an open-source Hebrew grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) system that outputs fully-specified International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcriptions, designed by augmenting a base diacritizer. (2) The ILSpeech corpus of paired Hebrew audio, text, and expert IPA annotations. (3) A benchmark for the previously unmeasured task of Hebrew G2P conversion. (4) Hebrew audio-to-IPA models capturing previously disregarded phonetic details for automatic TTS evaluation. Our results show that Phonikud more accurately predicts Hebrew phonemes than prior methods, and that small, local TTS models with phonetic input from Phonikud approach large proprietary systems. We release our code, data, and models at https://phonikud.github.io.

items.title: Speech-Worthy Alignment for Japanese SpeechLLMs via Direct Preference Optimization
items.authors: Mengjie Zhao(SB Intuitions); Lianbo Liu(SB Intuitions); Yusuke Fujita(SB Intuitions); Hao Shi(SB Intuitions); Yuan Gao(SB Intuitions); Roman Koshkin(SB Intuitions); Yui Sudo(SB Intuitions)
items.abstract: SpeechLLMs typically combine ASR-trained encoders with text-based LLM backbones, leading them to inherit written-style output patterns unsuitable for text-to-speech synthesis. This mismatch is particularly pronounced in Japanese, where spoken and written registers differ substantially in politeness markers, sentence-final particles, and syntactic complexity. We propose a preference-based alignment approach to adapt Japanese SpeechLLMs for speech-worthy outputs: text that is concise, conversational, and readily synthesized as natural speech. To rigorously evaluate this task, we introduce SpokenElyza, a benchmark for Japanese speech-worthiness derived from ELYZA-tasks-100 with auditory verification by a native expert. Experiments show that our approach achieves substantial improvement on SpokenElyza while largely preserving performance on the original written-style evaluation. We release SpokenElyza to support future research on Japanese spoken dialog systems.

items.title: Knowing What to Stress: A Discourse-Conditioned Text-to-Speech Benchmark
items.authors: Arnon Turetzky(The Hebrew University of Jerusalem); Avihu Dekel(IBM Research); Hagai Aronowitz(IBM Research); Ron Hoory(IBM Research); Yossi Adi(The Hebrew University of Jerusalem)
items.abstract: Spoken meaning often depends not only on what is said, but also on which word is emphasized. The same sentence can convey correction, contrast, or clarification depending on where emphasis falls. Although modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems generate expressive speech, it remains unclear whether they infer contextually appropriate stress from discourse alone. To address this gap, we present Context-Aware Stress TTS (CAST), a benchmark for evaluating context-conditioned word-level stress in TTS. Items are defined as contrastive context pairs: identical sentences paired with distinct contexts requiring different stressed words. We evaluate state-of-the-art systems and find a consistent gap: text-only language models reliably recover the intended stress from context, yet TTS systems frequently fail to realize it in speech. We release the benchmark, evaluation framework, construction pipeline and a synthetic corpus to support future work on context-aware speech synthesis.
