items.title: Cross-Lingual Compositional Learning for Code-Switched Lip Reading
items.authors: Jeonghyeon Joo(Ewha Womans University); Jiyoung Lee(Ewha Womans University)
items.abstract: Code-switching, the alternation of multiple languages in an utterance, is pervasive in multilingual communication but underexplored in visual speech recognition (VSR). Especially, the burden of collecting large-scale and realistic videos has limited the advances in code-switched VSR. We propose CoCoVSR, a cross-lingual compositional learning framework that exploits monolingual corpora. Specifically, without additional data collection or generative synthesis, CoCoVSR adapts a pretrained multilingual VSR model to code-switched scenarios, while preserving shared articulatory features. Experimental results show that CoCoVSR achieves SOTA on Chinese-English CSLR. Importantly, CoCoVSR achieves competitive performance on both seen (MultiVSR Chinese) and unseen (LRS2 English) multilingual datasets, highlighting its capability to preserve multilingual performance with negligible degradation. The code is available at https://github.com/ewha-mmai/CoCoVSR.

items.title: Refining Pseudo-Audio Prompts with Speech-Text Alignment for Text-Only Domain Adaptation in LLM-Based ASR
items.authors: Ryo Magoshi(Kyoto University); Takashi Maekaku(LY Corporation); Yusuke Shinohara(LY Corporation)
items.abstract: LLM-based automatic speech recognition models demonstrate strong performance by connecting audio encoders and LLMs. However, data scarcity of paired speech and transcription often hinders the adaptation to new domains, making text-only domain adaptation crucial. Existing methods typically rely on either fine-tuning the LLM alone or employing pseudo-audio prompts. The former neglects essential acoustic context, while the latter either suffers from limited scalability in data-scarce conditions, or yields inexpressive prompts by leveraging only textual features, ignoring audio modality. To address this, we propose a framework that explicitly models speech-text alignment. Our method efficiently generates highly expressive pseudo-audio prompts that bridge the modality gap, enabling effective target-domain adaptation. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing text-only methods, improving both overall error rates and out-of-vocabulary coverage.

items.title: Content-Aware Dynamic Compression for Efffcient Speech Recognition based on Large Language Model
items.authors: Huifeng Zhu(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Bingqian Wang(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Shaoxun Xiu(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Xingqun Jiang(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Bin Lv(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Current LLM-based speech recognition systems use fixed-rate downsampling for acoustic representation, which overlooks speech content dynamics and causes information loss or redundancy. We propose a content-aware dynamic acoustic map-ping method via the Continuous Integrate-and-Fire (CIF) mechanism, adaptively aligning speech embeddings with transcription token counts. This enables content-guided downsampling during training and inference, cutting LLM input length while preserving or boosting accuracy. On AISHELL-1 and Lib-riSpeech, we achieve 12-26% relative error reduction at comparable average speech embedding length (ASEL). While main-taining comparable performance, we achieve over 45% ASEL reduction with 7-19% lower time to first token (TTFT) across utterance lengths. GigaSpeech results confirm scalability. Our work establishes an efficient paradigm improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in LLM-based speech recognition.

items.title: Upcycling Pretrained Transformers into Mixture-of-Experts for Multilingual Speech Recognition
items.authors: Kentaro Shinayama(NTT); Kohei Matsuura(NTT); Jaeyoung Lee(NTT); Masato Mimura(NTT)
items.abstract: Fine-tuning large pretrained models is a powerful way to obtain high-accuracy systems for downstream ASR tasks. However, when fine-tuning on highly diverse data, such as multilingual corpora, performance can degrade compared with training separate models per language, largely due to limited model capacity. In this paper, we propose a simple capacity expansion method for multilingual fine-tuning by upcycling the feed-forward network (FFN) components of a pretrained model into a post-hoc Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. This conversion substantially increases the model's representational capacity while preserving inference efficiency: at test time, we activate only a single upcycled FFN expert, keeping the number of active parameters identical to the original dense model. We investigate two expert selection strategies: (1) hard routing based on language identity, and (2) soft routing using a learned router. Experiments on 10-language speech recognition with CommonVoice and additional ASR evaluations on four Asian languages demonstrate that the proposed upcycling-to-MoE approach consistently improves multilingual fine-tuning effectiveness.

items.title: Token-Independent Language Representations for Low-Latency Configurable Multilingual Speech Recognition
items.authors: Hongxu Zhu(Fano); Lahiru Samarakoon(Fano); Ivan Fung(Fano)
items.abstract: Configurable multilingual speech recognition enables a single model to be tailored to any user-selected language combination via language-specific modules (LSMs). While providing state-of-the-art accuracy, it incurs high latency as decoder LSMs are executed at every step, leading to extra computational costs that scale linearly with the output token length. To eliminate this per-token overhead, we propose token-independent language representations that decouple language identity from the autoregressive decoding loop. We replace the neural LSMs in the decoder with language representations enriched by one-time, utterance-level encoder cues. This reduces the LSM’s per-token complexity from quadratic to linear relative to the hidden dimension, while preserving utterance-level adaptability. Experiments show that our method achieves accuracy comparable to the original design while maintaining a near-constant LSM’s overhead, reducing peak inference latency by over 90% for long utterances.

items.title: GC-LoRA: Gated Convolutional LoRA for Parameter-Efficient Acoustic Adaptation
items.authors: Natarajan Balaji Shankar(University of California Los Angeles); Zilai Wang(University of California Los Angeles); Kaiyuan Zhang(University of California Los Angeles); Mohan Shi(University of California Los Angeles); Abeer Alwan(University of California Los Angeles)
items.abstract: Transformer-based Speech Foundation Models excel in most Automatic Speech Recognition tasks but often suffer performance degradation when applied to domains with mismatched acoustic characteristics. While Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods, such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), adjust global attention, they lack the local context modeling crucial for capturing domain-specific variations. We propose GC-LoRA, a novel adapter architecture that injects Conformer-style local convolutional processing into pretrained Transformer encoders. By integrating a lightweight adapter to encoder attention output projections, our method efficiently captures local acoustic dependencies without disrupting pretrained global representations. Experiments across diverse datasets (acoustically-degraded, bandlimited, dialectal, child) demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving Word Error Rate (WER) reductions of up to 10.9% compared to baselines while adding minimal trainable parameters.

items.title: MambAdapter: Lightweight Mamba-Based Adapters for Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning in Speech and Audio
items.authors: Salman Hussain Ali(Université de Montréal; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Umberto Cappellazzo(Imperial College London); Mirco Ravanelli(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute)
items.abstract: Fine-tuning Transformer-based foundation models has become the dominant strategy for domain adaptation in audio and speech processing. To reduce the computational and memory costs of this process, parameter-efficient transfer learning (PETL) methods have been widely explored. Meanwhile, Mamba, a recent state-space model, has emerged as a promising alternative to Transformers for sequence modeling. In this work, we present MambAdapter, a parameter-efficient transfer learning approach that integrates Mamba into low-rank bottleneck adapters. Our design combines parameter sharing across adapters with the injection of a lightweight Mamba module, enabling more effective modeling of audio features. We demonstrate that MambAdapter matches or outperforms strong PETL baselines on four audio classification tasks and five speech recognition languages, even when operating under reduced parameter budgets.

items.title: PhonePrune: One-shot Phoneme-Aware Pruning for Large-scale ASR Models via Phoneme Set Generation and Calibration
items.authors: Minsik Lee(Dongguk University); Jihie Kim(Dongguk University)
items.abstract: Large-scale Automatic Speech Recognition Models face deployment challenges due to massive parameter counts. While one-shot pruning compresses them, conventional methods indiscriminately discard low-magnitude parameters, degrading fine-grained phonetic distinctions. We conceptualize the sub-networks of these delicate weights as the Phoneme Ticket Hypothesis, arguing they must be preserved. We propose PhonePrune to preserve these weights via Phoneme Set Generation and Phoneme-aware Calibration. Evaluated on LibriSpeech and Common Voice (English, Korean, Japanese) at 50% sparsity, PhonePrune demonstrates strong results specifically on the Korean and Japanese datasets, yielding 13.41% and 13.83% Word Error Rate reductions over Distil-Whisper, respectively. Our success stems from preserving fragile parameters shared by these languages, such as subtle spectral variations in Korean and precise temporal durations in Japanese.

items.title: Can Large Language Models Reliably Correct Errors in Low-Resource ASR? A Contamination-Aware Case Study on West Frisian
items.authors: Yun Hao(University of Groningen); Reihaneh Amooie(University of Groningen); Wietse de Vries(University of Groningen); Rik van Noord(University of Groningen); Martijn Wieling(University of Groningen)
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has improved substantially in recent years, yet performance remains limited for low-resource languages. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for improving ASR through generative error correction (GER), but their effectiveness in low-resource settings remains underexplored. In addition, it remains unclear to what extent data contamination influences the reported improvements in LLM-based GER. This study investigates LLM-based GER for low-resource Frisian. In addition to a public corpus, we construct and use a Frisian offline dataset with non-public texts for evaluation to control for potential data contamination. Results show that GER improves ASR performance in most settings, with the best GPT-5.1 results surpassing oracle WERs. Comparable gains on the offline dataset indicate that improvements reflect true correction ability. We further provide a detailed error analysis revealing model correction patterns.

items.title: Contrastive Time-Proximity Pre-Training for Speech-Based Heart Failure Monitoring
items.authors: Tobias Fiedler(Noah Labs GmbH; University of Potsdam); Mariam Fouad(Noah Labs GmbH); Marcus Hott(Noah Labs GmbH); Leonhard Riehle(Noah Labs GmbH); Felix Hohendanner(German Heart Center of the Charité (DHZC)); Bruce Johnson(Mayo Clinic); Nicholas Cummins(King's College London); Bert Arnrich(University of Potsdam)
items.abstract: Heart failure (HF) causes recurrent acute decompensation (ADHF) requiring hospitalization. Fluid overload affects the vocal tract, making voice a potential non-invasive biomarker for early decompensation detection. Prior work used features from sustained vowels, relying on active patient engagement, limiting real-world applicability. We propose contrastive time-proximity (CTP), a self-supervised method learning HF-predictive representations from natural speech. CTP trains a segment-attentive LSTM to minimize embedding distances for recordings < 3 days apart (presumed similar health) while maximizing them for > 100 days apart (presumed different), exploiting HF's progressive nature. On a two-center dataset (68 ADHF patients), classical acoustic features achieve similar within-center accuracy but fail cross-center. CTP features suggest more robust cross-center generalization, outperforming random and human baselines. Attention analysis reveals focus on breathing-related segments.

items.title: Lung-CL: Spectrum-aware Distillation and Generative Replay for Continual Learning based buffer-free Respiratory Sound Classification
items.authors: Qinben Lai(Hebei University of Technology); Lukui Shi(Hebei University of Technology); Jiaxin Zhao(Macao Polytechnic University); Wenjuan Wang(Hebei University of Technology); Shuai Liu(Hebei University of Technology)
items.abstract: Real-world respiratory sound classification faces performance degradation from domain shifts in heterogeneous clinical scenarios. While Continual Learning (CL) aims to alleviate catastrophic forgetting, it faces challenges regarding data privacy and the failure to handle audio-specific spectral characteristics. In this paper, we propose Lung-CL, a unified framework for buffer-free domain incremental respiratory sound classification. It incorporates a Class-Specific Latent Replay strategy that synthesizes pseudo-features from learned distributions, and a Multi-Level Spectrum-Aware Distillation mechanism that disentangles pathological patterns from domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on three heterogeneous datasets (ICBHI, SPRSound and HF) show that Lung-CL significantly outperforms the existing continual learning methods in terms of classification accuracy and anti-forgetting ability.

items.title: An auscultation location specific study on the relationship between expiratory-to-inspiratory acoustic patterns and spirometric airflow limitation across age and gender in asthmatic patients
items.authors: Dheeraj Harish Kumar(Indian Institute of Science); Sanjana MC(Indian Institute of Science); Perumal Keerthi Priya(Indian Institute of Science); K V Nikhath Khanam(Indian Institute of Science); Uma Maheshwari Krishnaswamy(St. Johns National Academy of Health Sciences); Prasanta Kumar Ghosh(Indian Institute of Science)
items.abstract: Asthma causes expiratory airflow limitation and is clinically assessed using spirometry, which provides the FEV₁/FVC ratio representing the proportion of air exhaled in the first second relative to total forced vital capacity. Prior studies suggest that respiratory sounds recorded at posterior sites (Left Lower, Left Upper, Right Upper, Right Lower) reflect regional airflow patterns. In this study, we investigate the relationship between the expiratory-to-inspiratory (E/I) spectral power ratio and FEV₁/FVC in 141 participants aged 20-60 years using Spearman correlation across frequency subbands. The 100-200 Hz and 200-400 Hz bands showed significant correlations. Overall, lower posterior sites showed stronger associations; younger adults showed stronger correlations at the Left Lower site, whereas older adults showed stronger correlations at the Left Upper site. Gender-stratified analysis showed stronger Left Lower correlations in males and stronger Left Upper correlations in females.

items.title: Common Cold Corpus: Health-aware robustness study of modern speaker embeddings under physiological domain shift
items.authors: Anabell Hacker(Otto von Guericke University; University Hospital Magdeburg); Ingo Siegert(Otto von Guericke University; University Hospital Magdeburg)
items.abstract: This study investigates the impact of the common cold on speech using a new ecologically valid corpus. The Common Cold Corpus comprises paired recordings of 85 German speakers, collected remotely via personal devices during acute upper respiratory tract infections and healthy states. Unlike prior lab-based datasets focussing on severe cases, this corpus captures moderate symptoms in everyday acoustic environments. We evaluate eGeMAPS features against modern speaker embeddings (ECAPA2, TitaNet, ReDimNet). While acoustic analysis reveals consistent downward trends in pitch and harmonics-to-noise ratio when ill, only few features survive alpha-error correction. In contrast, speaker embeddings exhibit significant, directed displacement in the identity space under moderate symptomatology. Results suggest that neural models constitute a valuable, more sensitive addition to prosodic analyses, providing a robust foundation for non-invasive digital biomarkers in realistic settings.

items.title: Moot-Court: Training-Free Dialectical Reasoning for Depression Detection
items.authors: Yuqing Sun(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Jian Zhao(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Haoxun Li(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Leyuan Qu(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Taihao Li(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)
items.abstract: Automated depression screening is critical for alleviating medical resource shortages. While Large Language Models (LLMs) advance risk assessment, current methods rely on costly fine-tuning, risking overfitting. To address these challenges, we propose Moot-Court, a training-free reasoning engine inspired by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). By integrating clinical transcripts with textualized acoustic features, Moot-Court prompts a frozen LLM to conduct a simulated court debate, executing dialectical reasoning grounded in clinical symptom networks. Furthermore, we introduce Codex, a dynamic, self-evolving experience library updated via a training-free, reward-based feedback algorithm, explicitly constraining the LLM's reasoning trajectory to suppress hallucinations and enforce accuracy. Experiments on DAIC-WOZ show Moot-Court surpasses fine-tuned models, providing a robust, training-efficient solution.

items.title: Who is Speaking or Who is Depressed? A Controlled Study of Speaker Leakage in Speech-Based Depression Detection
items.authors: Hsiang-Chen Yeh(Johns Hopkins University); Luqi Sun(Johns Hopkins University); Aurosweta Mahapatra(Johns Hopkins University); Shreeram Suresh Chandra(Johns Hopkins University); Emily Mower Provost(University of Michigan); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University)
items.abstract: This study investigates whether speech-based depression detection models learn depression-related acoustic biomarkers or instead rely on speaker identity cues. Using the DAIC-WOZ dataset, we propose a data-splitting strategy that controls speaker overlap between training and test sets while keeping the training size constant, and evaluate three models of varying complexity. Results show that speaker overlap significantly boosts performance, whereas accuracy drops sharply on unseen speakers. Even with a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network, a substantial performance gap remains. These findings indicate that depression-related features extracted by current speech models are highly entangled with speaker identity. Conventional evaluation protocols may therefore overestimate generalization and clinical utility, highlighting the need for strictly speaker-independent evaluation.

items.title: Adapting Self-Supervised Speech Representations for Cross-Lingual Dysarthria Detection in Parkinson's Disease
items.authors: Abner Hernandez(Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg); Eunjung Yeo(UT Austin); Kwanghee Choi(UT Austin); Chin-Jou Li(CMU); Zhengjun Yue(Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Rohan Kumar Das(Fortemedia); Jan Rusz(Czech Technical University in Prague); Mathew Magimai Doss(Idiap Research Institute); Juan Rafael Orozco-Arroyave(FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg; Universidad de Antioquia); Tomás Arias-Vergara(FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg; Universidad de Antioquia); Andreas Maier(FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg); Elmar Nöth(FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg); David R. Mortensen(CMU); David Harwath(UTexas Austin); Paula Andrea Perez-Toro(Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg; Universidad de Antioquia)
items.abstract: The limited availability of dysarthric speech data makes cross-lingual detection an important but challenging problem. A key difficulty is that speech representations often encode language-dependent structure that can confound dysarthria detection. We propose a representation-level language shift (LS) that aligns source-language self-supervised speech representations with the target-language distribution using centroid-based vector adaptation estimated from healthy control speech. We evaluate the approach on oral diadochokinesis recordings from Parkinson's disease speech datasets in Czech, German, and Spanish under both cross-lingual and multilingual settings. LS substantially improves sensitivity and F1 in cross-lingual settings, while yielding smaller but consistent gains in multilingual settings. Representation analysis further shows that LS reduces language identity in the embedding space, supporting the interpretation that LS removes language-dependent structure.

items.title: Foundational speech models evaluation on multilingual dementia prediction
items.authors: Bartłomiej Eljasiak(Samsung R&D Institute); Wojciech Szecówka(Samsung R&D Institute; AGH University of Kraków); Piotr Masztalski(Samsung R&D Institute; AGH University of Kraków); Agnieszka Pruszek(Samsung R&D Institute; Koźmiński University); Teresa Brzozka(Samsung R&D Institute); Zofia Marciniak(Samsung R&D Institute); Justyna Krzywdziak(Samsung R&D Institute; AGH University of Kraków); Michał K. Grzeszczyk(Samsung R&D Institute); Łukasz Łazarski(Samsung R&D Institute); Mateusz Matuszewski(Samsung R&D Institute); Daria Hemmerling(Samsung R&D Institute; Harvard Medical School; AGH University of Kraków)
items.abstract: Dementia is neurological disorder that causes loss of cognitive functions primarily in older adults. Early dementia detection is essential to ensure professional treatment and increase the quality of life of affected people. In this paper, we propose a multilingual approach to the diagnosis of dementia with the use of speech foundational models. We investigate the effectiveness of using acoustic multilingual features for cognitive impairments detection. The work evaluates several popular speech foundational models such as Whisper, WavLM, Hubert, Wav2Vec2 with custom downstream heads. This pipeline is trained in single or multilingual settings and additionally evaluated on unseen languages to test their zero shot capabilities of predicting dementia. This pipeline achieves results of 0.854 F1 score average on combined English datasets and 0.761 F1 score in broader, more challenging multilingual setting.

items.title: Who Synthesized This? Joint Deepfake Detection and Generative Source Attribution
items.authors: Vishal Kumar(IIIT-Delhi); Vinayak Abrol(IIIT-Delhi); Mathew Magimai Doss(IDIAP Switzerland)
items.abstract: We propose a few-shot, open-set framework for joint deepfake detection and generative source attribution. Addressing the rapid evolution of synthetic speech, we introduce a temporal evaluation strategy using the MLAAD v9 dataset, partitioning models by launch year and architectural family. Our model utilizes a WavLM-Large model with targeted LoRA adapters, optimized via-a hierarchical metric learning objective: Conditional AAM Softmax + Center Loss. We simulate real-world forensic deployment by performing prototype-based inference on unseen 2025+ model families, establishing new class centroids with only 12 samples. Evaluated on the ASVspoof 5.0 benchmark, our framework achieves SOTA performance with 0.49% EER and 0.09 minDCF, while attaining 99% accuracy in tracing generated speech to its source. These results demonstrate that hierarchical representation learning and few-shot prototype adaptation provide a robust, scalable defense against the shifting landscape of audio synthesis.

items.title: Towards Digital Preservation of Efik: TTS for a Low-Resource African Language
items.authors: Offiong Bassey Edet(University of Cross River State; ML Collective); Emmanuel Oyo-Ita(University of Cross River State); Archibong Okon Archibong(University of Calabar); David Effanga Bassey(University of Calabar); Mbuotidem Sunday Awak(ML Collective)
items.abstract: Efik, a tonal language spoken by about 3 million second language speakers and 1.5 million native speakers in Southeastern Nigeria, remains underrepresented in speech synthesis research. We present the first documented end-to-end text-to-speech study for Efik, introducing a curated single speaker corpus of 2,632 utterances totaling three hours and a comparative evaluation of four neural models (VITS, MMS-TTS, SpeechT5, and Orpheus-TTS) under low resource conditions. Native speakers evaluated the systems using MOS, Nat-MOS, and A-MOS. MMS-TTS achieved the highest MOS of 3.80 ± 0.63 and produced more stable long form speech, though tonal errors persisted. Other models showed greater tonal and prosodic inconsistencies. These results provide a reproducible baseline and highlight the need for larger corpora and tone aware modeling for tonal African languages.

items.title: Rethinking Consent Acquisition for Voice Synthesis: from Static to Dynamic Consent
items.authors: Matilde Nanni(University of Inland Norway)
items.abstract: Voice synthesis raises specific ethical challenges by enabling third parties to generate speech in a person's voice without their involvement or control. Existing safeguards focus on consent acquisition, typically through contractual agreements, and attempt to regulate this practice via standard data-processing models of authorisation. However, voices function not only as data but also as markers of personal identity. As a result, one-time authorisation of voice data, which cannot be de-identified, leaves later uses insufficiently regulated and does not prevent identity-based harms to the original voice sources. This paper critically examines two models of contractual consent acquisition, one general and one specific, to show that neither satisfies the requirements for informed consent. As an alternative, the paper proposes dynamic consent, a type of informed consent that has been used in bioethics, as a governance solution better suited for synthetic voices.

items.title: Ethical and Technical Limits of Deepfake Speech Datasets
items.authors: Vojtěch Staněk(Brno University of Technology); Eva Trnovská(Brno University of Technology); Kamil Malinka(Brno University of Technology); Anton Firc(Brno University of Technology)
items.abstract: Claims about the robustness and fairness of deepfake speech detectors are only as credible as the datasets used to train and evaluate those systems. We present a dataset-level audit of the deepfake speech landscape. We compile and analyze 39 deepfake speech datasets, examining key attributes including accessibility, documentation, demographic and language coverage, dataset scale, and the underlying bona fide speech sources. Our audit reveals two important takeaways. Firstly, fairness assessment is largely infeasible because most datasets lack demographic metadata, and only a few contain gender or language labels. This prevents any meaningful subgroup analysis and leaves other demographic attributes unaddressed. Secondly, we identify substantial overlap in underlying bona fide source corpora across datasets, which can undermine cross-dataset evaluation and lead to overstated generalization claims.

items.title: AI Regulation and the Technical Language of Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Jennifer Williams(University of Southampton)
items.abstract: Speech synthesis has garnered increasing interest with global efforts to regulate artificial intelligence (AI), including deepfakes. Policymakers must draft careful wording to prevent societal harm and identify responsible parties. Legal AI provisions must be accurate, especially when instructing responsible parties to act, as seen in the transparency obligations across current AI regulations worldwide. But AI and generative AI are broad terms, and analogies from image and video domains do not translate well to speech. Current AI policy focussing on speech synthesis outputs overlooks portable models and complex workflows wherein speaker embeddings that encode voice identity can be developed independently and later repurposed. This paper traces the convergence of text-to-speech, voice conversion, speaker verification, and speech recognition, highlighting where legal definitions may fail to capture the technical components that enable voice cloning.

items.title: Tone-Conditioned Curriculum Learning for Low-Resource Bantu Speech Recognition
items.authors: Kesego Mokgosi(Technological University Dublin); Vukosi Marivate(University of Pretoria; Lelapa AI); Sitwala Mundia(University of Pretoria); Unarine Netshifhefhe(University of Pretoria); Tsholofelo Mogale(University of Pretoria); Thapelo Sindane(University of Pretoria)
items.abstract: Southern Bantu languages are spoken by over 80 million people, yet current foundation ASR models still produce zero-shot WER above 100%, which limits practical use in education and public services. We addressed this gap with a tone conditioned curriculum framework for 6 Southern Bantu languages that combined hybrid difficulty scoring, gated adapters driven by tonal statistics and staged curriculum training. We trained on a community corpus and tested transfer to NCHLT to measure robustness beyond matched evaluation. Results revealed clear interactions between architecture and language, with W2V-BERT outperforming Whisper on Nguni languages by 3 to 4 WER points whilst Whisper performed better on Sotho-Tswana languages. W2V-BERT with tone conditioning reached 28.41% average WER across datasets and 23.79% on Xitsonga transfer. No single model suited all 6 languages, so deployment should pair model selection per language with validation across corpora.

items.title: Which Languages Transfer Best to Warlpiri? A Similarity-Based Study for Low-Resource ASR
items.authors: Pravina Mylvaganam(University of New South Wales); Eliathamby Ambikairajah(University of New South Wales); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Tuende Szalay(University of Sydney)
items.abstract: This paper investigates how language similarity can improve cross-lingual transfer for automatic speech recognition (ASR) in extremely low-resource settings. Warlpiri, an Australian Aboriginal language, has very limited transcribed speech data, making transfer learning essential. We propose a framework combining acoustic similarity from pre-trained speech models with linguistic similarity based on typology, phoneme inventories, grammatical, and syntactic features to rank high-resource source languages and evaluate their effectiveness for ASR transfer to Warlpiri. Experiments with Whisper show that acoustically and typologically similar languages outperform monolingual and multilingual baselines. Assamese and Hindi achieve substantial reductions in word and character error rates. Correlation analysis further indicates that acoustic similarity is the strongest predictor of fine-tuning performance, while phoneme inventory and typological similarity better explain zero-shot transfer.

items.title: From Academic Tool to Community Infrastructure: A Call for Indigenous Partnership in Speech Data Governance
items.authors: Kaveri K. Sheth(PSL University); Sebastien Christian(UPF, CNRS)
items.abstract: We present ELSI (ExELang Legacy Support Interface), a governance platform for managing sensitive child-centered audio datasets that includes recordings from 10 indigenous language communities across multiple continents. While ELSI was designed to balance open science with participant privacy, we identify a fundamental gap: custodianship concentrates control in the hands of European academic researchers, with no formal plan for indigenous communities to govern their own data. We describe the platform, map its current model against CARE and OCAP principles, and issue a concrete call for indigenous community partners to co-design a framework for identifying legitimate community custodians and implementing an enforceable access and control layer. We commit to the architectural and governance changes needed to make this real, and describe what meaningful co-design would look like in practice.

items.title: Indigenising Speech Technology: Building a TTS Model for te Reo Māori
items.authors: Gianna Leoni(Te Hiku Media); Peter-Lucas Jones(Te Hiku Media); Tūreiti Keith(Te Hiku Media); Suzanne Duncan(Te Hiku Media)
items.abstract: This paper introduces an Indigenous-led approach for creating a high-quality text-to-speech (TTS) model for the Māori language (the Indigenous language of Aotearoa, New Zealand). The paper focuses on data curation, collection, and quality assurance, and the decisions made throughout that process, as examples of how this process could be replicated for other Indigenous, endangered, or minority languages. Despite the common assumption that the more data a model has, the better it will perform, this study demonstrates that meticulous attention to detail produces high-quality data and better results for Indigenous languages.

items.title: ‘I have to talk proper white ways’: Australian Aboriginal English Speakers’ Experiences with Voice Technologies
items.authors: Celeste Rodríguez Louro(University of Western Australia); Glenys Dale Collard(University of Western Australia); Hope Narrier(University of Western Australia); Katrina Cox(University of Western Australia); Lily Hayward(University of Western Australia); Daniel Colbung(University of Western Australia); Ben Hutchinson(Google Australia)
items.abstract: This article reports on a qualitative study investigating experiences of Indigenous people in Australia with voice technologies. Many Indigenous people in Australia speak Australian Aboriginal English, a variety which emerged as a result of forced contact between Indigenous communities and English speakers. It is widely used, yet is poorly supported by language technologies. Through Indigenous-led in-depth interviews, this research explores user experiences, attitudes, responses, and challenges encountered while interacting with various speech-enabled devices and applications using Australian Aboriginal English. We find that Indigenous users of ASR-powered technologies report poor experiences with the technologies, which they see as working better for non-Indigenous people. They report switching to speak like white people to get better ASR performance. Our findings reveal significant pressure to speak 'white way' when interacting with technology.

items.title: Two-stage semi-supervised learning with pseudo-labels: A case study on Northern Sámi ASR
items.authors: Priyanshi Pal(Aalto University; Instituto Superior Técnico); Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University); Kristiina Ojala(Aalto University); Tamás Grósz(South East Technological University); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)
items.abstract: While Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has advanced Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), limited labeled data remains a bottleneck for under-resourced languages, and smaller, parameter-efficient models underperform larger counterparts given equal supervised data. We explore semi-supervised learning with SSL models for Northern Sámi, an under-resourced agglutinative language. We compare two approaches: (i) all pseudo-labels generated by a teacher model and (ii) a subset from WER-based multi-teacher agreement. We show that a larger teacher improves out-of-domain generalization of a smaller model by 3.8-33.3% relative CER with no additional labeled data. With comparable data volume, the student benefits as much from pseudo-labels as from human-labeled data. For combining human and pseudo-labeled data, two-stage fine-tuning outperforms single-step mixed training. Overall, we show that lightweight models can approach larger models' performance even after a single pseudo-labeling iteration.

items.title: Pashto Common Voice: Building the First Open Speech Corpus for a 60-Million-Speaker Low-Resource Language
items.authors: Hanif Rahman(Pashto DAO); Shafeeq ur Rehman(Pashto DAO)
items.abstract: We present the Pashto Common Voice corpus — the first large-scale, openly licensed speech resource for Pashto, a language with over 60 million native speakers largely absent from open speech technology. Through a community effort spanning 2022-2025, the corpus grew from 1.5 hours and 5 contributors to 147 total hours and 1,483 unique speakers across ten Mozilla Common Voice releases (CV14-CV23). Speaker participation increased approximately 108-fold between CV17 and CV18, coinciding with a VOA Pashto broadcast campaign. We describe the full methodology: interface localisation, Wikipedia-based sentence extraction with automated filtering, phonemically targeted contributions for the four most frequently dropped Pashto characters, and multi-channel community outreach. MCV23 contains 107,781 clips (60,337 validated; 82.33 validated hours) across 13 content domains. Fine-tuning Whisper Base on the MCV20 yields 13.4% WER on the MCV20 test split, against the published Whisper Base zero-shot WER of 99.0% on Pashto.

title: Speech and Language Learning Technologies

items.title: Amadea: An AI Companion for Pitch-Aware Spoken Language Practice
items.authors: Mrigendra Agrawal(The University of Queensland; Amadea); Ryan Tsui(Amadea; University of Edinburgh); Kyaw Maung Maung Tet Toe(Amadea)
items.abstract: We present Amadea: an interactive speech learning platform for pitch-sensitive languages, including pitch accent languages such as Japanese and lexical tonal languages such as Mandarin. The system pairs an AI companion interface with real-time pronunciation feedback. When a learner speaks, the system transcribes the input and generates a native reference equivalent audio of the phrase. The system aligns the two audio files and compares their normalised fundamental-frequency (F0) contours to produce a pitch-pattern score. A graph visualising any pitch divergence throughout the phrase is then presented to the user. Amadea supports structured lessons as well as open-ended companion dialogue, with real-time feedback on both.

items.title: Real-Time CARFAC/SAI-derived Pitchogram for Seeing and Correcting Pronunciation in Mandarin Chinese Tones
items.authors: Yuka Maruyama(University of New South Wales); Jason Orlosky(Augusta University); Chris Lee(Georgia Institute of Technology); Flora Salim(University of New South Wales); Thad Starner(Georgia Institute Technology); Benjamin Tag(University of New South Wales)
items.abstract: We present a Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) system that incorporates a CARFAC (Cascade of Asymmetric Resonators with Fast-Acting Compression) and SAI (Stabilised Auditory Image)-derived pitchogram as an alternative to conventional spectrogram-based visualisation, which often fails to clearly represent temporal fine structure. The system features a dual-screen interface that provides real-time pitchogram feedback alongside reference pitchograms generated using Google Text-to-Speech. This design enables learners to perceive and produce the four Mandarin tones by comparing their speech with reference patterns. Our approach highlights the potential of pitchogram-based visualisation to support intuitive, real-time pronunciation practice for second language (L2) learners.

items.title: AURORA: A Web-based Authoring System for Bridging Aural-Oral Language Training and Communicative Practice
items.authors: Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: AURORA is a web-based authoring system for designing and deploying aural-oral training and communicative practice. For aural training, shadowing and its variants were implemented, and listening disfluency (LD) was measured and visualized. For oral training, imitative overlapping and its variants were used to quantify pronunciation deviations (PD) in learners' speech. For communicative practice, learners engaged in task-based oral conversations with ChatGPT, followed by prompt-based automatic assessment. With AURORA, two-month, inter-semester courseware was provided, where learners practiced for about 30 minutes per day to improve their listening, speaking, and communicative skills. This courseware supported university students during the transition to English-medium instruction, as more courses are offered in English. Training outcomes were evaluated objectively using LD and PD and subjectively through questionnaires. A tutorial workshop on AURORA was held for teachers in February.

items.title: VoxKit: Desktop Phone Alignment and Goodness of Pronunciation Analysis
items.authors: Nina R Benway(University of Maryland - College Park); Beckett Frey(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Tristan Mahr(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Michael McAuliffe(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Prad Kadambi(Arizona State University); Visar Berisha(Arizona State University); Katherine Hustad(University of Wisconsin - Madison)
items.abstract: VoxKit is an extensible desktop workbench that addresses a gap in available tools: no desktop application integrates forced alignment and goodness of pronunciation analysis in a single pipeline, creating a barrier to adoption for speech researchers working with clinical populations. With VoxKit, researchers can register datasets, select and train alignment engines, generate and compare alignments, and compute phone-level goodness of pronunciation scores within a single interface.

items.title: AdaptLingo: A Speech-to-Speech English Practice System with Fluency-Adaptive Responses
items.authors: Zackary Rackauckas(Columbia University)
items.abstract: We demonstrate AdaptLingo, an open-source, speech-to-speech English conversational agent for second-language learners. Beginners may be overwhelmed by many static language learning systems, which use complex language and fast speech, while advanced learners may disengage from simplified dialogue. AdaptLingo addresses this problem by predicting a learner's spoken fluency from temporal acoustic features, constraining responses to the learner's EIKEN-aligned vocabulary level, and adapting text-to-speech rate. In demonstration, users speak to the chatbot and receive spoken responses adapted to beginner, intermediate, or advanced fluency. Preliminary evaluation shows fluency classification works well on labeled data but remains challenging on noisy user-study speech, and user feedback suggests that adaptive spoken practice is promising when matched to learner background and conversational goals.

items.title: lisero: An interactive practice app for learning Romanian Sign Language
items.authors: Anisia Popescu(Université Paris 8; Fundatia CODA); Serban Din(Solid Technologies; Fundatia CODA); Marinela Axinte(Universitatea Babeş-Bolyai; Fundatia CODA)
items.abstract: Romanian Sign Language (LSR) was officially recognized in 2020, yet it remains severely under-resourced and insufficiently supported in educational contexts, including special education. Accessible and interactive learning tools are limited. We present, lisero, a freely accessible mobile app designed to support learning LSR through structured lessons and interactive exercises. Originally developed to support infant-caregiver interactions and support bimodal bilingualism, the app has been extended to cover general LSR learning scenarios. lisero features lesson-based content, practice exercises, and a growing sign dictionary. Gamification elements, as well as options to save and share signs, aim to enhance user engagement and community participation. The system is designed for both hearing users and deaf and hard-of hearing learners.

items.title: SayCheck: Gamified Speech Practice and Attribute-Based Speech Analysis for Children
items.authors: Mostafa Shahin(University of New South Wales); Kirrie Ballard(University of Sydney); Beena Ahmed(University of New South Wales)
items.abstract: This paper presents SayCheck, an AI-powered speech therapy platform designed to support children's speech practice through engaging gameplay and automated speech analysis. The platform combines two integrated components: Say Bananas, a Mario-style speech therapy game that motivates home practice, and PhoneAid, an automatic speech analysis system that evaluates children's speech productions at both the phoneme and phonological attribute levels. The system enables therapists and caregivers to configure targeted speech exercises while providing detailed diagnostic feedback about pronunciation performance. PhoneAid extends traditional phoneme-level assessment by analysing articulatory and phonological speech attributes, allowing more informative feedback about how speech sounds differ from target productions. A demonstration of the system highlights the workflow from gameplay-based speech elicitation to detailed automatic speech assessment and summary reporting.

items.title: A Speech-First Character Interface for Stylized Japanese Dialogue Practice
items.authors: Zackary Rackauckas(RoleGaku)
items.abstract: We present Jouzu, a mobile Show & Tell demonstration of expressive persona-conditioned spoken interaction for Japanese language practice. In Jouzu, attendees choose a fictional character, type or speak a prompt, hear a character-specific Style-BERT-VITS2 voice response, compare how multiple personas realize the same utterance through wording, register, and speech, and tap unfamiliar Japanese words for in-place reading support. The demo foregrounds speech as the primary medium for experiencing persona, affect, and learner feedback, rather than treating audio as an add-on to a text chatbot. This paper describes the runnable interaction loop, persona-conditioned generation, expressive TTS pipeline, speech-input path, comparison mode, and booth workflow that combine LLM dialogue, character voice synthesis, and vocabulary scaffolding in a live Japanese-practice system.

items.title: CodeVaani: A Multilingual, Voice-Based Code Learning Assistant
items.authors: Jayant Havare(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Srikanth Tamilselvam(IBM Research India); Ashish Mittal(Google DeepMind India); Shalaka Thorat(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Soham Jadia(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Varsha Apte(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Ganesh Ramakrishnan(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay)
items.abstract: Programming education often assumes English proficiency and text-based interaction, creating barriers for students in non-English speaking countries like India. We present CodeVaani, a multilingual voice-enabled code assistant built into IIT Bombay’s Learning Management System, helping learners explore programming concepts in their native languages. The system integrates Indic ASR, a code-aware transcription refinement, and a code model to generate responses in both text and audio. In a study with 28 beginner programmers, over 89% rated the experience as fair or above. CodeVaani offers on-demand, scalable, multilingual support, lowering the entry barrier for students with limited English proficiency and demonstrating how voice-based AI can make programming education more inclusive. Supplementary artefacts and demo video are available.

items.title: Auditory Contrast Network for Text-Free Prominence Detection
items.authors: Kosuke Shimizu(University of Tsukuba); Keiichi Zempo(University of Tsukuba)
items.abstract: We introduce the Auditory Contrast Network (ACN), a model with up to 238 trainable parameters that encodes three psychoacoustic principles - pairwise contrast, cue independence, and forward dominance - into an interpretable detector of word-level perceived prominence. Using only three acoustic features and no text, ACN achieves r = 0.412 on cross-corpus transfer (Helsinki Prosody → Emphases), matching a frozen 94.6M-parameter wav2vec2 baseline (r = 0.409) at 120× lower latency; adding text features raises r to 0.451. The learned weights suggest forward-dominant context use (over 96% preceding across all cues), strict locality (±1 word), and the cue hierarchy duration > energy > spectral ≫ F0, consistent with established findings while preserving a direct architectural readout. The acoustic-only result makes ACN suitable for on-device applications where text is unavailable, such as hearing aids and real-time pronunciation monitoring.

items.title: F0 realization of prosodic focus across adulthood in Jianghuai Mandarin
items.authors: Xinxian Zhao(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Xiaohu Yang(Tongji University)
items.abstract: This study examined age-related variation in the F0 realization of prosodic focus across adulthood in Jianghuai Mandarin. A focus production task was conducted with young, middle-aged, and older adult speakers, who produced sentences with neutral focus and three types of narrow focus. The results show that Jianghuai Mandarin exhibits the canonical tri-zone F0 pattern, reflected in both mean F0 and F0 excursion, and that this global pattern is largely preserved across age groups. However, fine-grained F0 adjustments, i.e., the contrast between narrow and neutral focus, show age-related variation. In particular, older speakers demonstrate greater post-focus compression in mean F0 compared with young and middle-aged speakers. These findings indicate that prosodic focus across adulthood is characterized by stable global F0 patterning but age-sensitive fine-grained F0 adjustment.

items.title: Prosodic Realization of Focus in Yi-Mandarin Bilingual Speakers: On-Focus Expansion without Post-Focus Compression
items.authors: Ziyu Zhang(Flinders University); Chenyu Li(Johns Hopkins University)
items.abstract: Post-focus compression (PFC) is absent in Yi (Nuosu), a Tibeto-Burman tone language, but present in Beijing Mandarin. We examined whether Yi-Mandarin bilingual speakers produce PFC in L2 Mandarin, using delta-F0 and intensity as primary measures and duration as a secondary measure, across initial, medial, and final focus conditions. Yi speakers produced on-focus F0 expansion fully comparable to Beijing controls, yet showed no post-focus compression across all conditions in both F0 and intensity. Individual variation in Mandarin language background did not predict post-focus F0 among Yi speakers. These results demonstrate a complete dissociation between intact on-focus expansion and absent post-focus compression, suggesting that when the L1 entirely lacks PFC, the mechanism may be suppressed in L2 production even under prolonged bilingual contact-consistent with the view that on-focus expansion and post-focus compression constitute functionally independent prosodic modules with distinct acquisition trajectories.

items.title: The (non-)universality of prominence and Intonation Phrases: German and Hungarian listeners' perception of an unfamiliar language
items.authors: Farhat Jabeen(Bielefeld University); Ákos Buza(Bielefeld University); Ella Reimann(Bielefeld University)
items.abstract: This study adopts a typological perspective to examine the nonuniversality of acoustic cues used to perceive prosodic prominence and Intonation Phrase (IP) boundaries. By using speech extracts from an unfamiliar language, we analyse the role of acoustic cues beyond the lexical and pragmatic factors. Employing Rapid Prosody Transcription, we presented speech extracts from Urdu to German and Hungarian listeners who were asked to identify prominent words and IP boundaries. We found that listener groups relied on different F0 contours and scaling patterns to perceive prominence. Moreover, they exhibited variable inter- and intra-rater agreement when identifying IP boundaries. By presenting the same Urdu stimuli to listeners of typologically diverse languages, we offer a nuanced perspective to investigate within- and between-group (dis)agreement. This sheds light on language-specific and cross-linguistic variability in the perception of prosodic phenomena.

items.title: Broad Focus Rise(-fall) Declaratives in Venetan: Investigating Typological Outliers in Italo-Romance Intonation
items.authors: Elinor Payne(University of Oxford); Angelo Dian(University of Oxford)
items.abstract: Intonational rises in unmarked declaratives are cross-linguistically rare. While reported for Venetan (an Italo-Romance variety spoken in north-eastern Italy), little is known about their properties, or indeed Venetan intonation in general. To address this, we investigate the prevalence, distribution and properties of intonational rise(-falls) in broad focus declaratives in gambellarese, a central-western Venetan dialect, for semi-spontaneous speech. We find rise(-falls) to be roughly as common as falls, and to occur regardless of position of lexical stress, strongly indicating the existence of an alternative unmarked rising nuclear tune for declaratives, distinct from the H+L* L% tune reported for Italian and other Italo-Romance varieties. We also examine the phonetic effects of word-final stress (common in Venetan) on tonal alignment with regard to these rise(-falls).

items.title: Should Robots Sound more like Machines than like Humans? User Expectations Affect the Perception of Prosody in TTS Voices
items.authors: Ha Eun Shim(Simon Fraser University; University of Massachusetts Amherst); Paige Tuttösí(Simon Fraser University; Enchanted Tools); Olivia Yung(Simon Fraser University); Ivan Fong(Simon Fraser University); Sara Ng(Simon Fraser University); Angelica Lim(Simon Fraser University); Yue Wang(Simon Fraser University); H. Henny Yeung(Simon Fraser University; CNRS & Université Paris Cité)
items.abstract: Prosodic and indexical features of artificial voices, like naturalness, tone, and emotion, are often treated as distinct from intelligibility. Yet prosody can be critical: Consider, "She has to pull Bart" (without commas/prosodic boundaries) versus "She has to pull, Bart" (with commas/prosodic boundaries). Here, we asked how humans disambiguated such sentences while listening to a robot avatar, as prosodic and indexical features in the robot voice were manipulated. Prosodic pitch changes to make the voice either affective or monotonic had little effect on intelligibility. Surprisingly, indexical changes to increase machine-like (and less human-like) voice quality, despite being phonetically irrelevant to this prosodic contrast, increased intelligibility, but only for sentences with commas. Results imply that hearing machine-like voices changes listener expectations, biasing or pushing listeners to hear prosodic boundaries (i.e., commas) that are otherwise hard to detect.

title: Source Separation 1

items.title: WeSep: A Modular and Cue-Composable Framework for Target Speaker Extraction
items.authors: Ke Zhang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xiaoyang Yu(Nanjing University); Haoyu Li(Nanjing University); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Shuhan Zhang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Haizhou Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute)
items.abstract: The study of Target Speaker Extraction (TSE) aims to isolate a desired speaker from overlapping speech mixture given auxiliary cues. Existing systems are typically designed for specific cue types, limiting flexibility when cue availability varies across scenarios. We present WeSep, a unified framework that reformulates TSE as a heterogeneous cue-conditioned learning problem. In WeSep, cue modules and separator backbones are decoupled through standardized interfaces, enabling configurable cue injection and flexible integration of diverse modalities. The design enables systematic study of cue structure, intra-and cross-modal interaction, and dynamic cue availability within a shared optimization framework, facilitating adaptation to real-world conditions. Experiments across enrollment, spatial, visual, and textual cues reveal modality-dependent characteristics and demonstrate stable optimization under heterogeneous cue availability. The toolkit is publicly available.

items.title: TF-MoE: Time-Frequency Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Speech Separation
items.authors: Qinzhe Hu(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Chenda Li(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Wangyou Zhang(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Shujie Liu(Microsoft Research Asia); Yan Lu(Microsoft Research Asia); Yanmin Qian(Shanghai Jiaotong University)
items.abstract: Recent advances in speech separation (SS) have led to compact front-end models with small parameter sizes, yet their high computational cost remains a major barrier for deployment on edge devices. To address this, we propose TF-MoE, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances model capacity with almost no increase in inference cost. Our method introduces dynamic expert specialization in time and frequency dimensions through alternating time-wise and frequency-wise MoE modules, each dynamically selecting experts per frame or mel band. Built upon a mel-band-splitting Conformer backbone, TF-MoE achieves strong performance on SS tasks under low-compute settings. Experimental results demonstrate that TF-MoE consistently improves separation performance under computation cost constraints, outperforming BSRNN by +3.8 dB SDR on Libri2Mix with comparable 4.1 GMACs/s inference cost. This positions TF-MoE as a promising candidate for edge-device deployment.

items.title: Sweep-RSE: Streaming Region-of-Interest Speech Extraction in Multi-Talker Scenarios via Explicit Spatial Sweeping
items.authors: Hogeon Yu(Hyundai Motor Company); SeongHun Noh(Hyundai Motor Company); Hyunsik Choi(Hyundai Motor Company); Sihyun Joo(Hyundai Motor Company)
items.abstract: Region-of-Interest (ROI) speech extraction is crucial for AR/VR and hearing aids but challenging in streaming multi-talker scenarios. Existing methods rely on implicit boundary conditioning, often failing to isolate targets under dense interference or suppress noise in empty regions. We propose Sweep-RSE, a lightweight, fully causal framework utilizing an explicit Align & Sweep mechanism. By actively scanning the ROI, our model locks onto target signals via phase coherency and explicitly models spatial discrepancies to reject outliers. Integrated with a Region Speech Detector, it ensures real-time O(1) processing. Experiments demonstrate Sweep-RSE achieves precise target extraction in complex scenarios and effectively suppresses false alarms in silent regions, operating efficiently with only 1.66M parameters and 3.05 GMACs.

items.title: Online Audiovisual Speaker Separation Using Efficient Visual Knowledge Distillation
items.authors: Cheng Yu(The Ohio State University); Vahid A. Kalkhorani(The Ohio State University); Ashutosh Pandey(Meta Reality Labs); Daniel Wong(Meta Reality Labs); Jacob Donley(Meta Reality Labs); Buye Xu(Meta Reality Labs); DeLiang Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: We present an efficient visual knowledge distillation (VKD) strategy to address the causal audiovisual speaker separation (AVSS) problem. Causal AVSS systems suffer from significant performance degradation due to the absence of the future context and the reliance on heavily parameterized visual embedding models originally developed non-causally. VKD progressively transfers knowledge from a causally inferred pre-trained visual front-end to a lightweight, task-oriented student model via a dynamic weighting mechanism, preserving speaker-discriminative embeddings while reducing overall system complexity. VKD compresses the visual front-end by more than 48 times in model size and 7.5 times in computational complexity. Through extensive comparisons, evaluations, and ablation studies on multiple datasets, we demonstrate that VKD combined with a top-performing online AVSS separator achieves the state-of-the-art causal AVSS performance.

items.title: DTT-BSR+: A Generative-Regression Cascade for Music Source Restoration
items.authors: Youran Ni(Wuhan University); Shihong Tan(Wuhan University); Yuzhu Wang(Tampere University); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University)
items.abstract: Music source restoration (MSR) requires jointly addressing source unmixing and the inversion of non-linear production effects. Current methods struggle to achieve accurate target signal reconstruction while maintaining semantic consistency. To address this limitation, we propose DTT-BSR+, a two-stage cascade MSR system that decouples distribution fitting from signal reconstruction into separate stages. A generative DTT-BSR separator in the first stage produces stems matching the prior of clean sources, and a modified Demucs network in the second stage enhances the first stage output using time-domain and multi-resolution spectral losses. DTT-BSR+ improves multi-mel signal-to-noise ratio (MMSNR) over the single-stage DTT-BSR across all stems, and surpasses the state-of-the-art X-LANCE MSR system on five stems. We also reveal through Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD) decomposition an implicit trade-off between signal reconstruction accuracy and semantic distribution fitting across stems.

items.title: Adaptive Hard-Pair Sampling via Curriculum Learning for Speech Separation
items.authors: Pengjie Shen(Inner Mongolia University; Southern University of Science and Technology); Xueliang Zhang(Inner Mongolia University); Zhong-Qiu Wang(Southern University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: End-to-end neural speech separation systems have achieved strong average scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR) scores, yet still struggle with mixtures where speakers have highly similar timbre. These difficult cases reduce robustness and raise concerns about real-world generalization. To address this, we propose a curriculum hard-pair sampling strategy. During training, a pairwise speaker-speaker difficulty matrix is built and updated online based on the SI-SDR score of separating each speaker pair. Each mixture for model training is constructed by first randomly sampling an anchor speaker, and the interference speaker is sampled based on a temperature-controlled Softmax which gives more weights to speakers that are, as indicated by the difficulty matrix, difficult to be separated with the anchor speaker. Results on Libri2Mix show that the proposed method consistently improves performance, especially for similar-timbre mixtures, without additional training overhead.

title: Real-Time, Low-Latency and Edge Speech Enhancement
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 6 - Oral 3 - Real-Time, Low-Latency and Edge Speech Enhancement

items.title: HALO: Half-Frame-Rate Adaptive Learnable Operator for Lightweight STFT-Based Speech Enhancement
items.authors: Jiadong Zhao(Nanjing University); Dahan Wang(Nanjing University); Yu Sun(Samsung Electronics); Leyan Yang(Nanjing University); Xiaobin Rong(Nanjing University); Shiruo Sun(Horizon Robotics); Yuxiang Hu(Horizon Robotics); Jing Lu(Nanjing University)
items.abstract: STFT-based speech enhancement typically adopts overlapping analysis frames. While overlap is essential for stable STFT processing, it makes adjacent frames highly correlated, causing redundant computation in lightweight models. We propose Half-frame-rate Adaptive Learnable Operator (HALO), a causal plug-in module that halves the internal frame rate without altering the STFT procedure. Broadly applicable to many lightweight models, HALO applies adaptive rate reduction before the backbone and restoration afterward, reconstructing the full-rate spectrum on the original STFT grid. Both reduction and restoration are implemented with lightweight dynamic convolutions. By halving the processed frame rate, HALO reduces backbone compute cost with no added algorithmic latency, freeing budget for channel widening. Experiments on the DNS3 dataset show consistent gains across diverse lightweight models under matched complexity, demonstrating the effectiveness of reducing overlap-induced redundancy.

items.title: Latency-Configurable Streaming Speech Enhancement via Asymmetric Temporal Padding
items.authors: Yunsik Kim(POSTECH); Yoonyoung Chung(POSTECH; Intus Co. Ltd.)
items.abstract: Streaming speech enhancement requires balancing algorithmic latency against quality, yet existing approaches largely treat this as a binary causal versus non-causal choice. LaCo-SENet addresses this issue with two mechanisms parameterized by a single training-time hyperparameter. First, asymmetric temporal padding redistributes past and future context in convolutions, enabling systematic latency configuration. Second, dual-buffer streaming combines state buffers for past context with lookahead buffers that supply future context at both the input and feature levels. Selective state updates also prevent future-frame leakage into the streaming state, ensuring training-inference consistency. On VoiceBank+DEMAND, a fixed-budget (1.37M parameters) backbone yields a family of models spanning 12.5-75.0 ms, with PESQ rising from 3.35 to 3.43. At just 12.5 ms (fully causal), a PESQ of 3.35 matches or exceeds the prior causal state-of-the-art (3.27 at 46.5 ms).

items.title: Latency Controllable Speech Enhancement
items.authors: Hiroshi Sato(NTT, Inc.); Takafumi Moriya(NTT, Inc.); Tsubasa Ochiai(NTT, Inc.); Marc Delcroix(NTT, Inc.)
items.abstract: Streaming speech enhancement must meet latency budgets ranging from a few milliseconds (for hearing devices) to hundreds of milliseconds (for telephony/offline applications). Since latency–quality is a trade-off, an enhancer should exploit as much lookahead as the budget allows; yet most neural models are trained for a single fixed lookahead, so multiple budgets usually require multiple full models. We propose a latency-controllable speech enhancement framework consisting of a causal enhancement model augmented with Latency Control Adapters (LCAs) that allow switching the model's latency by changing how much future context it can exploit. With intra-batch multi-latency training, one LCA model supports seven latency modes; it surpasses per-latency models in enhancement quality, maintains constant inference MACs, and reduces stored parameters by 76%.

items.title: Real-Time Speech Enhancement on Edge Devices Guided by Harmonic and Voice-Activity Cues Utilizing Skin-Attachable Accelerometer
items.authors: Yonghun Song(POSTECH); Yeongmin Kim(Intus Co., Ltd.); Yunsik Kim(POSTECH); Yeeun Kim(POSTECH); Yoonyoung Chung(POSTECH; Intus Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Skin-attachable accelerometers (ACCs) capture noise-robust speech vibrations and complement acoustic microphones (AMs). However, multimodal speech enhancement models combine ACC and AM signals with parallel encoders or attention blocks, which increases edge-deployment cost. We present a lightweight ACC-assisted U-Net v2 (LAU-NetV2) based on efficient cue-guided feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). The ACC stream is compressed into temporal voice activity to suppress non-speech regions and spectral harmonics to preserve voiced structures. These speech-informative representations generate FiLM parameters that modulate intermediate feature maps in the time-frequency domain. The LAU-NetV2 with FiLM has 46k parameters, 68× fewer than prior multimodal models. ACC-guided modulation improves PESQ from 1.78 to 2.78 on TAPS+DNS and outperforms baselines. Finally, the LAU-NetV2 runs in 48.66 ms on a wearable microcontroller prototype, enabling real-time voice interfaces.

items.title: RT-SEMamba: Real-Time Speech Enhancement Mamba via Progressive Knowledge Distillation
items.authors: Rong Chao(National Taiwan University; Academia Sinica); Sung-Feng Huang(NVIDIA); Moreno La Quatra(Kore University of Enna); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(University of Palermo); Wen-Huang Cheng(National Taiwan University); Szu-Wei Fu(NVIDIA); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica)
items.abstract: We present RT-SEMamba, a fully causal speech enhancement (SE) model built upon causal time-frequency Mamba blocks. Unlike Transformer-based architectures that rely on a growing key-value cache, Mamba propagates a fixed-size recurrent state per layer, enabling memory- and bandwidth-efficient long-form inference. We further introduce a progressive knowledge distillation (KD) strategy that compresses an 8-layer teacher into a shallow 1-layer student by jointly distilling complex spectral outputs and intermediate representations. On Voicebank-DEMAND, the 8-layer RT-SEMamba achieves 3.32 PESQ with a 25 ms algorithmic latency constraint, and the distilled 1-layer student improves over a naive 1-layer baseline from 3.06 to 3.18 PESQ while preserving the same steady-state RTF, delivering a 2.75× speedup over the teacher. These results demonstrate that state-space models with progressive KD provide a competitive quality-latency trade-off for real-time SE.

items.title: RT-Tango: Real-Time Distributed Binaural Speech Enhancement for Low-Power Hearing Aid Devices
items.authors: Zahra Benslimane(Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, List ; Universite de Lorraine, CNRS, Inria, LORIA); Pierre Chouteau(Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, List); Martyna Poreba(Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, List); Fabrice Auzanneau(Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, List); Michal Szczepanski(Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, List); Fabian Chersi(Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, List); Romain Serizel(Universite de Lorraine, CNRS, Inria, LORIA)
items.abstract: Real-time binaural speech enhancement is constrained by latency, computational cost, and inter-device communication, yet existing efficient solutions predominantly address single-channel settings. In this paper, we introduce RT-Tango, a real-time distributed binaural speech enhancement framework designed for streaming on resource-constrained platforms and specifically for hearing aids. RT-Tango relies on a two-stage distributed architecture combining perceptually motivated ERB feature compression, lightweight grouped recurrent mask estimation, and temporal sparsification to reduce computational cost. Stringent latency constraints are addressed by decoupling spectral resolution from algorithmic delay using an asymmetric STFT, together with causal recurrent inference and online estimation of spatial statistics. Experimental results show that RT-Tango achieves competitive speech enhancement while significantly reducing MACs operations and functioning at ultra-low latencies as low as 8 ms.

items.title: ViP-VL: Vietnamese Self-supervised Speech Pretraining Model with Vector-Quantization Learning
items.authors: Khanh Le(VinUniversity); Kiet Anh Hoang(UNEY); Bao Nguyen(UNEY); Duy Vo(UNEY); Dung Vo(UNEY); Thai Tran(UNEY); Linh Pham(UNEY); Khoa D Doan(VinUniversity)
items.abstract: We present ViP-VL, an efficient Vietnamese Self-supervised speech Pretraining model leveraging Vector-quantization Learning. To bridge the gap between high-resolution audio and efficient processing, ViP-VL incorporates Acoustic Stacking and Receptive Field Alignment to enable a synchronized 8x subsampling rate within the ChunkFormer architecture, while further enhancing representation robustness through a specialized Mask Selection Strategy during pretraining on the BEST-RQ framework. Pretrained on 17,000 hours of unlabeled Vietnamese speech, our model establishes new state-of-the-art results across four major downstream tasks: Automatic Speech Recognition, Speech Emotion Recognition, Dialect Classification, and Speaker Verification. To facilitate future research and the development of high-performance Vietnamese speech technologies, we publicly release our pretrained weights and implementation at github.com/khanld/chunkformer.

items.title: Dissecting ASR Failures in Low-Resource South Asian Languages
items.authors: Abdul Hameed Azeemi(Lahore University of Management Sciences); Ihsan Ayyub Qazi(Lahore University of Management Sciences); Maryam Mustafa(Lahore University of Management Sciences); Agha Ali Raza(Lahore University of Management Sciences)
items.abstract: Urdu, Punjabi, Pashto, and Sindhi, spoken by over 350 million people, pose unique ASR challenges: closely related Perso-Arabic scripts, unstandardized orthography, and mixed-script named entities. We evaluate five multilingual ASR models on two benchmarks using an 11-category error taxonomy. Script confusion drives the majority of Whisper's failures on three of four languages. SeamlessM4T achieves the best results (16.3% WER on Urdu, 22.1% on Punjabi), though still far from production-grade accuracy. Cross-language contamination affects up to 35% of output characters in lower-resource languages; rare words reach only 20-62% accuracy; and short utterances are harder than long ones, reversing the high-resource pattern. Standard WER conflates recognition errors with orthographic and Unicode variation, overstating rates by up to 3.1 points. Transliteration post-processing recovers up to 25 points of WER without retraining. Our findings provide actionable guidance for ASR in this language family.

items.title: Vividh-ASR: A Complexity-Tiered Benchmark and Optimization Dynamics for Robust Indic Speech Recognition
items.authors: Kush Juvekar(Adalat AI); Kavya Manohar(Adalat AI); Aditya Srinivas Menon(Adalat AI); Arghya Bhattacharya(Adalat AI); Kumarmanas Nethil(Adalat AI)
items.abstract: Fine-tuning multilingual ASR models like Whisper for low-resource languages often improves read speech but degrades spontaneous audio performance. To diagnose this mismatch, we introduce Vividh-ASR, a complexity-stratified benchmark for Hindi and Malayalam across four tiers: studio, broadcast, spontaneous, and synthetic noise. Through a controlled study of learning-rate timing and curriculum ordering, we find that early large parameter updates improve global WER by ~12 absolute points, while a hard-to-easy curriculum adds gains for spontaneous speech. These findings motivate reverse multi-stage fine-tuning (R-MFT), a training recipe that enables a parameter-efficient 244M Whisper model to match or exceed conventionally fine-tuned 769M counterparts. Representational analysis via CKA and SVD reveals effective schedules concentrate adaptation in the decoder, preserving the pre-trained encoder's acoustic geometry. We release the benchmark and models.

items.title: Unified Gradient Projection: Language-Balanced Continual Learning for Multilingual Low-Resource ASR
items.authors: Ziang Ren(Tsinghua University); Guodong Lin(Tsinghua University); Yuchen Ai(Tsinghua University); Kaize Tan(Tsinghua University); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Large-scale pretrained ASR models such as Whisper exhibit strong multilingual capabilities. However, fine-tuning on low-resource languages often causes catastrophic forgetting. Although continual learning mitigates this issue, existing methods struggle to regulate cross-task interference in multilingual settings, where dominant languages bias optimization. We propose Unified Gradient Projection (UGP), which constrains parameter updates using reference gradients from language-balanced replay in a unified projection space. By equalizing per-language contributions in the projection, UGP reduces dominant-language bias and improves cross-lingual stability. We further show that combining gradient-level projection with data-level replay yields complementary gains in stability and plasticity. Across diverse low-resource language groups and model scales, UGP enables effective adaptation while substantially mitigating forgetting. On Whisper-large-v3, it achieves near-zero average forgetting.

items.title: Beyond Standard Greek: Adapting Whisper for Greek Dialects through Curriculum Multitask Learning
items.authors: Antigoni Klimi(Athena Research Center); Dimitrios Damianos(Athena Research Center); Stavros Bompolas(Athena Research Center); Vivian Stamou(Athena Research Center); Stella Markantonatou(Athena Research Center); Vassilis Katsouros(Athena Research Center); Georgios Paraskevopoulos(Athena Research Center)
items.abstract: In this work, we investigate training strategies for improved Whisper adaptation for Greek dialects under low-resource constraints. We propose a unified framework that integrates three pillars: data augmentation with an adjacent donor language, multitask learning (joint speech recognition and translation), and a staged curriculum. Our curriculum is implemented as a progressive training pipeline, beginning with cross-lingual translation and donor-language supervision, gradually transitioning to dialect-specific ASR. Empirical results across three distinct low-resource settings (Cypriot, Cretan, and Messenian) demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms conventional fine-tuning across various model scales. Furthermore, detailed ablations validate our design choices, confirming that the synergy between curriculum learning and multitask supervision is essential for effective adaptation.

items.title: Vimarsha: Faithful ASR Evaluation for Indian Languages with Demographic Diversity, In-the-Wild Audio and Spelling Variations
items.authors: Kaushal Bhogale(IIT Madras); Srija Anand(IIT Madras); Sadakopa Ramakrishnan Thothathiri(Sarvam AI); Tahir Javed(IIT Madras); Sshubam Verma(Sarvam AI); Mitesh Khapra(IIT Madras)
items.abstract: Evaluation benchmarks for Indian language automatic speech recognition (ASR) suffer from two systematic biases: optimistic scores from clean, controlled audio conditions, and pessimistic scores from overly rigid transcription standards that penalize valid linguistic variations. We introduce Vimarsha, a 100-hour benchmark spanning all 22 scheduled Indian languages, designed to address both distortions. Vimarsha combines demographically diverse on-field recordings with carefully mined in-the-wild audio selected for acoustic difficulty, alongside a lattice of variations framework that encodes multiple valid transcriptions per utterance. Evaluations of 10 state-of-the-art ASR models reveal substantial shifts in model rankings under realistic conditions, geographic and demographic performance disparities, and systematic failure modes across speaking rates and acoustic environments.
